# STATISTICAL METHODS FOR DATA SCIENCE
**Course Code:** STAT 350 | **Credits:** 3 | **Semester:** Fall 2024

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Schedule:**  
- - 
**Teaching Assistant:** [Name] | **TA Office Hours:** Monday/Wednesday 1:00-2:00 PM

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course provides undergraduate students with a comprehensive foundation in statistical concepts and methods essential for data science applications. Students will explore descriptive and inferential statistics, probability distributions, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and statistical modeling techniques commonly used in data-driven decision making. The course emphasizes practical application through hands-on analysis of real-world datasets from various domains including business, healthcare, and social sciences. 

Students will learn to interpret statistical results, assess data quality, and communicate findings effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences. Key topics include exploratory data analysis, correlation and causation, linear and multiple regression, ANOVA, chi-square tests, and bootstrap methods. The course integrates statistical theory with computational practice using statistical software packages. Students will develop critical thinking skills to evaluate statistical claims, design appropriate analyses for different data types, and understand the limitations and assumptions of statistical methods. 

This course serves as a crucial bridge between introductory statistics and advanced data science techniques, preparing students for careers in analytics, research, business intelligence, and graduate studies in data science or related fields.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Apply** descriptive and inferential statistical methods to analyze real-world datasets and draw meaningful conclusions for business and research applications

• **Evaluate** statistical assumptions and model validity through diagnostic plots, residual analysis, and goodness-of-fit tests using R and Python

• **Design** appropriate statistical tests and analyses by identifying data types, research questions, and selecting suitable methodologies for different scenarios

• **Communicate** statistical findings using visualization tools, written reports, and oral presentations tailored to diverse stakeholder audiences

## TARGET AUDIENCE & PREREQUISITES

**Target Audience:** Undergraduate students majoring in Data Science, Computer Science, Mathematics, Business Analytics, or related quantitative fields who seek to develop strong statistical foundations for data analysis careers or graduate studies. Ideal for students planning to work as data analysts, business analysts, research associates, or pursue advanced degrees in data science.

**Prerequisites:** 
- MATH 151 (Calculus I)
- STAT 201 (Introduction to Statistics) 
- CS 101 (Introduction to Programming) or equivalent

Students should have basic familiarity with algebraic concepts, fundamental programming logic, and introductory statistical concepts including measures of central tendency, variability, and basic probability.

---

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

**Textbooks:**
- *Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R* (2nd Edition) by James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani (Free PDF available)
- *Think Stats: Exploratory Data Analysis in Python* (2nd Edition) by Allen B. Downey (Free online)

**Software:** 
- R and RStudio (free download)
- Python 3.7+ with Anaconda distribution (free download)
- Jupyter Notebooks
- Access to university computing labs

**Online Resources:**
- Course management system (Canvas/Blackboard)
- Datasets provided via course repository
- Supplementary video lectures and tutorials

---

**Readings:** James et al. Ch. 1-2; Downey Ch. 1-3

---

**Assessment:** Discussion Board - Data Science Project Lifecycle Discussion **Due Week 4** (100 points)

**Readings:** Downey Ch. 4-6

---

*Statistical Graphics, Dashboard Design, Audience-Appropriate Communication*

---

*Bias-Variance Tradeoff, Cross-Validation, Statistical Power*

**Key Learning Activities:**

- **Week 14 Lab:** Interpreting Statistical Power and Effect Size Trade-offs in A/B Testing Scenarios (120 min)

**Assessment:** End-to-End Predictive Analytics Pipeline for Customer Churn Analysis **Due Week 14** (100 points)

**Readings:** James et al. Ch. 5

---

*Model Comparison, Business Context Evaluation, Ethical Considerations*

**Assessment:** End-to-End Predictive Analytics Project: Customer Churn Prediction with MLOps Implementation **Due Week 15** (100 points)

**Assessment:** End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline Implementation and Defense **Presentations Week 16** (100 points)

# Advanced Machine Learning for Large-Scale Data Systems
**Course Number:** CS 8XX | **Credits:** 4 | **Quarter:** Fall 2024

---

## Course Description

This graduate-level course explores cutting-edge machine learning techniques specifically designed for handling massive datasets and distributed computing environments. Students will delve into scalable algorithms, parallel processing frameworks, and cloud-based ML platforms while addressing real-world challenges in big data analytics. The curriculum covers advanced topics including distributed deep learning, federated learning, streaming analytics, and MLOps practices for production systems. Through hands-on projects using industry-standard tools like Apache Spark, Kubernetes, and cloud ML services, students will develop practical skills in designing, implementing, and deploying machine learning solutions at enterprise scale. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical applications, preparing students to tackle complex data science challenges in technology companies, research institutions, and data-driven organizations. Students will work with multi-terabyte datasets, implement fault-tolerant ML pipelines, and learn to optimize model performance across distributed clusters. By the end of the quarter, participants will have built a complete end-to-end ML system capable of processing real-time data streams and serving predictions at scale, while understanding the trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and computational resources in production environments.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement distributed machine learning algorithms to process datasets exceeding single-machine memory constraints using Apache Spark and Dask frameworks
• Evaluate and optimize model performance in production environments through systematic A/B testing, monitoring dashboards, and automated retraining pipelines
• Develop scalable data preprocessing and feature engineering workflows by implementing ETL pipelines on cloud platforms including AWS, GCP, and Azure
• Construct real-time machine learning systems using streaming technologies like Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, and containerization with Docker and Kubernetes

---

## Target Audience & Prerequisites

**Target Audience:** Graduate students in Data Science, Computer Science, or related fields seeking careers as Senior Data Scientists, ML Engineers, or Data Platform Engineers at technology companies, financial institutions, or research organizations. Ideal for students planning to work with large-scale data systems, pursue PhD research in machine learning, or transition into technical leadership roles requiring deep understanding of production ML systems.

**Prerequisites:** 
- Completion of undergraduate machine learning course or equivalent (CS 229/STAT 315 level)
- Proficiency in Python programming with experience in scikit-learn and pandas
- Solid foundation in linear algebra and statistics
- Familiarity with SQL and database concepts
- Basic experience with command-line tools and version control (Git)
- **Recommended:** Prior exposure to cloud computing platforms and containerization technologies

---

## Required Materials

### Textbooks
- **Primary:** *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly, 2017)
- **Reference:** *Hands-On Machine Learning* (3rd Edition) by Aurélien Géron (O'Reilly, 2022)

### Software & Platforms
- **Programming:** Python 3.9+, Jupyter Notebook/Lab

- **Tools:** Docker Desktop, Git, DBeaver or similar SQL client
- **Development Environment:** Access to university computing cluster or personal laptop with 16GB+ RAM

### Hardware Requirements
- Laptop capable of running virtual machines and containers
- Minimum 16GB RAM, 20GB available storage
- Reliable internet connection for cloud computing sessions

---

## Course Description

This graduate-level course provides comprehensive coverage of advanced machine learning techniques specifically designed for large-scale data analysis. Students will explore scalable algorithms, distributed computing frameworks, and cloud-based solutions essential for modern data science applications. The curriculum emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical implementation of machine learning models on big data platforms including Apache Spark, Hadoop ecosystem, and cloud services like AWS and Google Cloud Platform. 

Students will work with real-world datasets exceeding traditional computational limits, learning to optimize model performance, handle data preprocessing at scale, and deploy production-ready solutions. Key topics include ensemble methods, deep learning architectures for big data, stream processing, feature engineering at scale, and AutoML systems. The course bridges the gap between academic machine learning concepts and industry requirements, preparing students for senior data scientist and machine learning engineer roles.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement scalable machine learning algorithms to process datasets exceeding 100GB using distributed computing frameworks

• Evaluate and compare ensemble methods, deep learning architectures, and automated machine learning approaches by implementing comprehensive benchmarking studies  
• Deploy end-to-end machine learning pipelines using Apache Spark, MLflow, and containerization technologies like Docker and Kubernetes

# APPLIED STATISTICAL ANALYSIS FOR DATA SCIENCE
**Course Code:** DSCI 250  
**Credits:** 4 Quarter Hours  
**Quarter:** Fall 2024  

## INSTRUCTOR INFORMATION

**Teaching Assistant:** Marcus Johnson  
**Lab Office Hours:** TR 1:00-2:00 PM  

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course provides undergraduate students with essential statistical foundations and practical analytical skills required for modern data science applications. Students will learn to apply statistical methods to real-world datasets, interpret results meaningfully, and communicate findings effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on experience with statistical software, covering descriptive statistics, probability distributions, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and experimental design. Through project-based learning using authentic datasets from various domains including healthcare, business, and social sciences, students will develop critical thinking skills necessary for data-driven decision making. The course bridges theoretical statistical concepts with practical implementation, preparing students for advanced coursework in machine learning, predictive analytics, and specialized data science applications.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Evaluate and select** appropriate statistical methods to analyze diverse datasets for business and research applications  
• **Implement** hypothesis testing and regression analysis through hands-on practice with R and Python statistical libraries  
• **Construct** comprehensive statistical reports by combining analytical results with clear visualizations and written interpretations  
• **Design and execute** experimental studies using statistical sampling techniques and randomized controlled trial methodologies  

## PREREQUISITES

- Completion of Calculus I (MATH 151) with grade of C or better
- Introduction to Programming (CS 101 or equivalent)
- College Algebra (MATH 110)
- **Recommended:** Basic familiarity with spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets) and introductory statistics concepts

## TARGET AUDIENCE

Undergraduate students majoring in Data Science, Statistics, Computer Science, Business Analytics, or related quantitative fields who have completed foundational mathematics coursework and seek to develop practical statistical analysis skills for careers in data analysis, business intelligence, market research, or graduate studies.

---

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

### Textbooks
- **Primary:** *Practical Statistics for Data Scientists* (2nd Edition) by Bruce, Bruce, and Gedeck
- **Secondary:** *Python for Data Analysis* (3rd Edition) by Wes McKinney

### Software & Technology
- **Python 3.8+** with Anaconda distribution (free)
- **R and RStudio** (free)
- **Jupyter Notebooks** (included with Anaconda)
- **University Learning Management System** (Canvas)
- Personal laptop recommended for labs and projects

### Required Python Libraries
- pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn, plotly, scipy, statsmodels, scikit-learn

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### **Week 1: Course Introduction & Statistical Foundations**
- **Topics:** Course overview, statistical thinking, types of data, sampling methods
- **Readings:** Textbook Ch. 1-2
- 
### **Week 2: Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization**
- **Topics:** Descriptive statistics, data profiling, univariate and bivariate analysis
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Descriptive statistics (central tendency, dispersion, shape)
  - Data profiling and quality assessment
  - Correlation vs. causation principles
- **Activities:** 
  - *Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Statistical Visualization Analysis* (60 min)
  - *Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Behavior Data* (75 min)
- - **Readings:** Textbook Ch. 3-4

### **Week 3: Data Quality and Cleaning Strategies**
- **Topics:** Missing data handling, outlier detection, data validation techniques
- **Activities:**
  - *Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for Customer Survey Analysis* (110 min)
  - *Evaluating the Effectiveness of Data Cleaning Strategies on Dataset Quality* (120 min)
- - **Assessment:** Quiz 1 - EDA and Data Quality (25 points)

### **Week 4: Probability Distributions and Statistical Inference**
- **Topics:** Normal distribution, Central Limit Theorem, confidence intervals
- **Activities:**
  - *Interpreting Statistical Significance vs. Practical Significance in A/B Test Results* (70 min)
- - **Readings:** Textbook Ch. 5-6

### **Week 5: Hypothesis Testing Fundamentals**
- **Topics:** Null/alternative hypotheses, Type I/II errors, t-tests, chi-square tests
- **Activities:**
  - *Interpreting Confounding Variables in Observational Studies* (85 min)
- - **Assessment:Data Science Project Presentation** assigned (100 points, due Week 8)

### **Week 6: ANOVA and Experimental Design**
- **Topics:** One-way and two-way ANOVA, experimental vs. observational studies
- **Activities:**
  - *Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision Making* (60 min)
- - **Assessment:** Quiz 2 - Hypothesis Testing (25 points)

### **Week 7: Regression Analysis I - Simple and Multiple Linear Regression**
- **Topics:** Linear relationships, least squares, model assumptions, diagnostics
- **Activities:**
  - *Interpreting Feature Importance in Machine Learning Models* (85 min)
- - **Readings:** Textbook Ch. 7-8

### **Week 8: Regression Analysis II - Model Selection and Validation**
- **Topics:** Model selection criteria, cross-validation, multicollinearity
- **Activities:**
  - *Interpreting Cross-Validation Results to Compare Model Performance* (80 min)
  - *Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Analysis* (60 min)
- - **Assessment:Data Science Project Presentation** due (100 points)

### **Week 9: Introduction to Machine Learning for Statistics**
- **Topics:** Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, classification vs. regression
- **Activities:**
  - *Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Customer Churn Analysis* (3.5 hours)
  - *Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Fraud Detection* (90 min)
- - **Assessment:Customer Churn Prediction Project** assigned (100 points, due Week 11)

### **Week 10: Ethics and Bias in Data Analysis**
- **Topics:** Algorithmic bias, fairness metrics, responsible AI practices
- **Activities:**
  - *Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Fraud Detection* (165 min)
- - **Assessment:Ethics Discussion Forum** (100 points)
- **Readings:** Supplemental readings on AI ethics

### **Week 11: Final Projects and Review**
- **Topics:** Project presentations, course review, advanced topics preview
- **Assessment:Customer Churn Prediction Project** due (100 points)
- **Assessment:** Final Exam (100 points)

---

## ASSESSMENT PLAN

### Grade Distribution
| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage |
|----------------|--------|------------|
| Quizzes (2 × 25 points) | 50 | 11% |
| Data Science Project Presentation | 100 | 22% |
| Customer Churn Prediction Project | 100 | 22% |
| Ethics Discussion Forum | 100 | 22% |
| Final Exam | 100 | 22% |
| **Total** | **450** | **100%** |

### Assessment Descriptions

**Quizzes (50 points total)**
- Two timed assessments covering fundamental concepts
- Quiz 1: EDA and data quality (Week 3)
- Quiz 2: Hypothesis testing (Week 6)

**Data Science Project Presentation (100 points)**
Students will conduct a complete data science analysis on a provided dataset and present their findings through a 10-minute presentation. This assessment evaluates students' ability to apply the entire data science pipeline from data exploration to communicating insights to a non-technical audience.

**Customer Churn Prediction Project (100 points)**
Students will build a complete machine learning pipeline to predict customer churn for a telecommunications company, including data preprocessing, feature engineering, model development, evaluation, and business recommendations. This project assesses both technical data science skills and business communication abilities.

**Ethics and Bias Discussion Forum (100 points)**
Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing real-world case studies of algorithmic bias and ethical failures in machine learning systems, proposing comprehensive mitigation strategies and evaluating the societal implications of data science decisions.

**Final Exam (100 points)**
Comprehensive assessment covering all course material with emphasis on statistical interpretation and practical application.

### Grading Scale
- A: 90-100%
- B: 80-89%
- C: 70-79%
- D: 60-69%
- F: Below 60%

---

## COURSE POLICIES

### Attendance Policy
Regular attendance is essential for success in this course. Students are expected to attend all lectures and lab sessions. More than two unexcused absences may result in a reduction of the final grade. Students are responsible for obtaining notes and assignments from missed classes.

### Late Work Policy
- **Assignments:** 10% penalty per day late (including weekends)

All work submitted must be your own. Collaboration is encouraged on lab activities and discussions, but individual assignments and exams must be completed independently. Proper citation is required for all external sources. Violations will result in course failure and academic disciplinary action.

### Technology Policy
- Laptops and tablets are encouraged for note-taking and lab work
- Mobile phones should be silenced during class
- Use of technology should be course-related during class time

### Accommodation Statement
Students with documented disabilities who may need accommodations should make an appointment with the instructor as soon as possible. All discussions will remain confidential. Students with disabilities who are experiencing academic difficulties are encouraged to contact the Office of Disability Services.

### Communication Policy

## ADDITIONAL RESOURCES

# DATA VISUALIZATION AND STATISTICAL GRAPHICS
**Course Code:** DS 321  
**Credits:** 4 Quarter Credits  
**Prerequisites:** CS 141 (Introduction to Programming), STAT 201 (Introduction to Statistics), DS 201 (Fundamentals of Data Science)

**Class Schedule:**  
Lecture: MWF 10:00-10:50 AM, [Room]  
Lab: T 2:00-3:50 PM, [Computer Lab]

**Quarter:** [Term Year]

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course introduces students to the principles and practice of creating effective data visualizations for exploratory analysis, statistical communication, and data-driven storytelling. Students will learn to transform raw data into compelling visual narratives using industry-standard tools and programming libraries. The course covers visualization theory, including perception psychology and design principles, while providing hands-on experience with statistical graphics, interactive dashboards, and web-based visualizations. 

Students will work with real-world datasets from various domains including business, healthcare, and social sciences to create visualizations that reveal patterns, trends, and insights. Emphasis is placed on choosing appropriate chart types, designing for different audiences, and avoiding common visualization pitfalls. The course balances theoretical foundations with practical application, preparing students to communicate data findings effectively in professional settings. Projects include creating static visualizations, interactive dashboards, and presentation-ready graphics. Students will develop a portfolio of visualization work that demonstrates their ability to translate complex data into accessible visual stories.

**Target Audience:** Undergraduate students majoring in Data Science, Statistics, Computer Science, or related quantitative fields who have completed introductory programming and statistics courses. Ideal for students seeking careers in data analysis, business intelligence, market research, or any role requiring data communication skills.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design and implement effective statistical visualizations** to communicate complex data patterns and insights to diverse audiences  
• **Create interactive dashboards and web-based visualizations** through hands-on experience with Python libraries (matplotlib, seaborn, plotly) and Tableau  
• **Evaluate visualization effectiveness** by applying principles of visual perception, cognitive psychology, and information design theory  
• **Develop data storytelling capabilities** using R/ggplot2 and D3.js to create publication-quality graphics and interactive web visualizations

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

### Textbooks
- **Primary:** Wilke, C. O. (2019). *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*. O'Reilly Media. (Available free online)
- **Secondary:** Healy, K. (2018). *Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction*. Princeton University Press.

### Software & Tools
- **Python 3.8+** with Anaconda distribution
- **R and RStudio** (latest versions)
- **Tableau Desktop** (free student license)
- **Web browser** with developer tools
- **Git** for version control
- **Jupyter Notebooks** environment

### Hardware Requirements
- Laptop capable of running data analysis software
- Minimum 8GB RAM recommended
- Reliable internet connection for web-based visualizations

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### **Week 1: Foundation of Data Visualization and EDAModule:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Statistical Visualization

This module focuses on the critical process of Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), which serves as the foundation for all data science projects. Students will master the systematic approach to investigating data characteristics through statistical summaries and visual exploration techniques.

**Key Concepts:**
- Descriptive Statistics: Measures of central tendency, dispersion, skewness, and kurtosis
- Data Distribution Analysis: Assessing normality, identifying distribution types, and understanding variable behavior
- Correlation and Covariance: Statistical measures quantifying relationships between variables

**Learning Activities:**
- *Interpreting Data Distributions Through Real Estate Analysis* (110 min) - Students analyze housing price data to identify and interpret different distribution patterns
- Lab: Introduction to Python visualization libraries (matplotlib, seaborn)

**Deliverables:** Dataset selection for final project (due Friday)

---

### **Week 2: Understanding Data Relationships and QualityModule:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization (Continued)

Students will dive deeper into understanding relationships within data while developing skills to assess and address data quality issues that impact visualization effectiveness.

**Key Concepts:**
- Data Profiling: Systematic examination of dataset structure and completeness
- Univariate Analysis: Statistical summaries and visualizations for single variables
- Bivariate Analysis: Exploring relationships between variables using correlation analysis

**Learning Activities:**
- *Interpreting Correlation Matrix Patterns in Customer Behavior Data* (60 min) - Analysis of e-commerce correlation matrices
- *Evaluating Data Quality Issues in a Customer Dataset for Business Decision-Making* (85 min) - Critical assessment of data quality problems

**Deliverables:** Lab Report 1: EDA of chosen dataset (due Tuesday)

---

### **Week 3: Visualization Design Principles and EffectivenessModule:** Visual Design Theory and Perception Psychology

This week focuses on the theoretical foundations of effective data visualization, incorporating principles from cognitive psychology and design theory to create compelling visual narratives.

**Key Concepts:**
- Visual Perception Psychology: How humans process visual information
- Design Principles: Color theory, typography, spatial relationships
- Chart Selection: Matching visualization types to data types and analytical goals

**Learning Activities:**
- *Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making* (85 min) - Critical assessment of competing visualizations
- *Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Survey Results* (75 min) - Hands-on evaluation using structured frameworks

**Assessment:Midterm Exam** - Fundamentals of Data Science Concepts and Basic Analysis (100 points)

---

### **Week 4: Feature Engineering for Better VisualizationsModule:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning

Feature engineering skills are essential for creating meaningful visualizations. This module teaches students to transform raw data into formats that reveal important patterns and relationships through visual exploration.

**Key Concepts:**
- Feature transformation: Converting raw variables through scaling, encoding, and mathematical operations
- Feature selection: Identifying most predictive variables for visualization focus
- Dimensionality reduction: PCA and t-SNE for visualizing high-dimensional data

**Learning Activities:**
- *Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models* (100 min) - Understanding which features drive patterns
- Lab: Creating derived features for enhanced visualizations

**Deliverables:** Project Proposal: Visualization goals and approach (due Friday)

---

### **Week 5: Interactive Visualizations with PythonModule:** Advanced Python Visualization Techniques

Students will master creating interactive visualizations using plotly and build their first web-based dashboards, learning to engage audiences through dynamic visual experiences.

**Key Concepts:**
- Interactive Elements: Hover effects, zooming, filtering, and selection
- Dashboard Design: Layout principles and user experience considerations
- Web Integration: Embedding visualizations in web applications

**Learning Activities:**
- Hands-on lab: Building interactive dashboards with plotly Dash
- Workshop: Best practices for user interface design

**Deliverables:** Interactive Visualization Assignment (75 points, due Tuesday)

---

### **Week 6: Statistical Graphics with R and ggplot2Module:** Advanced Statistical Visualization

This week introduces R's powerful ggplot2 library for creating publication-quality statistical graphics, emphasizing the grammar of graphics approach to systematic visualization design.

**Key Concepts:**
- Grammar of Graphics: Systematic approach to visualization construction
- Statistical Transformations: Built-in statistical summaries and modeling
- Multi-panel Visualizations: Faceting and small multiples techniques

**Learning Activities:**
- *Understanding Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Analysis* (90 min) - Visualizing model performance concepts
- Lab: Creating publication-ready graphics with ggplot2

**Assessment:Lab Report** - Customer Churn Prediction Analysis (100 points, due Friday)

---

### **Week 7: Business Intelligence and TableauModule:** Enterprise Visualization Tools

Students learn industry-standard business intelligence tools, focusing on Tableau for creating executive dashboards and business reporting visualizations.

**Key Concepts:**
- Business Dashboard Design: KPI visualization and executive reporting
- Data Connections: Integrating multiple data sources
- Calculated Fields: Creating business metrics and derived measures

**Learning Activities:**
- *Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance* (180 min) - Comprehensive model comparison using visualizations
- Workshop: Tableau best practices and advanced features

**Deliverables:** Tableau Dashboard Assignment (75 points, due Tuesday)

---

### **Week 8: Web-Based Visualizations with D3.jsModule:** Advanced Web Visualization Technologies

Introduction to D3.js for creating custom, web-native visualizations that can be integrated into modern web applications and data products.

**Key Concepts:**
- D3.js Fundamentals: Data binding and DOM manipulation
- SVG Graphics: Scalable vector graphics for web visualizations
- Animation and Transitions: Creating engaging visual experiences

**Learning Activities:**
- *Interpreting Statistical Significance in A/B Testing Results* (120 min) - Visualizing statistical concepts
- Lab: Building custom D3.js visualizations

**Deliverables:** Mid-project check-in: Portfolio progress review

---

### **Week 9: Data Storytelling and CommunicationModule:** Visual Narrative and Audience Design

This week focuses on crafting compelling data stories for different audiences, learning to sequence visualizations effectively and communicate insights that drive decision-making.

**Key Concepts:**
- Narrative Structure: Beginning, middle, end in data presentations
- Audience Analysis: Tailoring visualizations for technical vs. non-technical audiences

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This foundational course introduces students to essential statistical concepts and methodologies used in data science applications. Students will learn to apply statistical techniques to real-world datasets, develop critical thinking skills for data interpretation, and gain hands-on experience with statistical software. The course covers descriptive statistics, probability distributions, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and statistical modeling. Emphasis is placed on understanding when and how to apply different statistical methods, interpreting results in context, and communicating findings effectively. Students will work with datasets from various domains including business, healthcare, social sciences, and technology to develop practical skills in statistical analysis. This course serves as a crucial foundation for advanced data science coursework and prepares students for entry-level analyst positions in industry. By the end of the semester, students will be equipped with the statistical literacy necessary to critically evaluate data-driven claims and conduct their own statistical investigations using modern computational tools.

---

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Analyze** complex datasets to identify patterns and relationships using descriptive statistics and data visualization techniques

# Advanced Topics in Algebraic Topology
**Mathematics 8XX • Graduate Level • [Semester/Quarter]**

---

## Course Description

This graduate-level course explores advanced concepts in algebraic topology, building upon fundamental knowledge of homology and cohomology theory. Students will delve into spectral sequences, characteristic classes, K-theory, and cobordism theory, with applications to differential geometry and mathematical physics. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and computational techniques, preparing students to engage with current research in topology and related fields. Topics include the Serre spectral sequence, Chern classes, vector bundles, and stable homotopy theory. Students will develop expertise in advanced topological invariants and their applications to classification problems in geometry and topology. The course includes a significant research component where students will read recent papers and present original investigations. This coursework is essential for students pursuing doctoral research in topology, algebraic geometry, or theoretical physics, and provides critical background for understanding modern developments in homotopy theory and its connections to number theory and representation theory.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Construct and compute spectral sequences to solve complex homological problems in algebraic topology and differential geometry
• Analyze characteristic classes and vector bundle theory through detailed calculations using Chern-Weil theory and obstruction theory
• Prove fundamental theorems in K-theory and cobordism by applying advanced techniques from stable homotopy theory
• Demonstrate research proficiency using contemporary mathematical software including SageMath and specialized topology packages for computational verification of theoretical results

## Target Audience

Second or third-year mathematics PhD students specializing in topology, geometry, or related areas, as well as advanced master's students planning to pursue doctoral studies. Students should have strong backgrounds in abstract algebra and point-set topology, with career goals in academic research, government research laboratories, or advanced positions in mathematical modeling and data science requiring sophisticated topological methods.

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations and Spectral Sequence Theory
**Topics:** Review of homological algebra; introduction to spectral sequences; convergence criteria
- **Monday:** Course introduction, prerequisites review, introduction to filtered complexes
- **Wednesday:** First quadrant spectral sequences, convergence theorems
- **Friday:** The Serre spectral sequence: construction and basic properties
- **Activity:** Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Resource Allocation (adapted for homological calculations)

### Week 2: The Serre Spectral Sequence
**Topics:** Fibrations and their spectral sequences; transgression; multiplicative structure
- **Monday:** Fibrations and path-loop fibration
- **Wednesday:** Computing with the Serre spectral sequence
- **Friday:** Applications: cohomology of Lie groups and homogeneous spaces
- **Assessment:** Problem Set 1 (spectral sequence computations) - Due Friday

### Week 3: Characteristic Classes I
**Topics:** Vector bundles; Chern classes; Stiefel-Whitney classes
- **Monday:** Vector bundles and principal bundles
- **Wednesday:** Construction of characteristic classes via obstruction theory
- **Friday:** Chern-Weil theory and differential forms
- **Activity:** Design Your Dream City adapted for bundle constructions over topological spaces

### Week 4: Characteristic Classes II  
**Topics:** Euler class; Pontrjagin classes; applications to differential geometry
- **Monday:** The Euler class and Gauss-Bonnet theorem
- **Wednesday:** Pontrjagin classes and signature theorem
- **Friday:** Characteristic classes and immersion problems
- **Assessment:** Midterm Examination - Advanced Calculus and Linear Algebra Integration Exam (adapted for topology)

### Week 5: K-Theory Foundations
**Topics:** Vector bundles and K⁰; Bott periodicity; K-theory of spheres
- **Monday:** The group K⁰(X) and basic operations
- **Wednesday:** Bott periodicity theorem (statement and consequences)
- **Friday:** K-theory of projective spaces
- **Activity:** Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow (adapted for K-theory computations)

### Week 6: Advanced K-Theory
**Topics:** Adams operations; splitting principle; Chern character
- **Monday:** Lambda operations and Adams operations
- **Wednesday:** The splitting principle and symmetric functions
- **Friday:** Chern character and Riemann-Roch theorem
- **Assessment:** Research Paper Topic Proposals Due

### Week 7: Cobordism Theory
**Topics:** Oriented cobordism; Thom spaces; Thom isomorphism theorem
- **Monday:** Manifolds and cobordism relations
- **Wednesday:** Thom spaces and Thom classes  
- **Friday:** The Thom isomorphism theorem
- **Activity:** Optimizing Manufacturing Production Using Linear Programming (adapted for cobordism calculations)

### Week 8: Stable Homotopy Theory
**Topics:** Spectra; stable homotopy groups; Freudenthal suspension theorem
- **Monday:** Suspension and loop functors; Freudenthal theorem
- **Wednesday:** Introduction to spectra
- **Friday:** Stable homotopy groups of spheres
- **Assessment:** Mathematical Problem-Solving Portfolio: Real-World Applications (adapted for topology applications)

### Week 9: Advanced Topics and Applications
**Topics:** Extraordinary cohomology theories; Atiyah-Singer index theorem; applications to physics
- **Monday:** Extraordinary cohomology and Brown representability
- **Wednesday:** The Atiyah-Singer index theorem (statement and applications)
- **Friday:** Topological quantum field theories and applications
- **Activity:** Personal Budget Creation Using Percentage Calculations (adapted for index computations)

### Week 10: Research Presentations
**Topics:** Student research presentations; current developments in the field
- **Monday-Wednesday-Friday:** Student research presentations (20 minutes each + discussion)
- **Assessment:** Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation: Exploring Open Problems in Algebraic Topology

---

## Assessment Plan

|----------------|--------|------------|-------------|
| Problem Sets (4) | 200 | 25% | Weekly computational problems and proofs |
| Midterm Exam | 100 | 12.5% | In-class examination covering spectral sequences and characteristic classes |

course_info.title: Functional Analysis and Operator Theory
course_info.description: This graduate-level course provides a rigorous introduction to functional analysis with emphasis on operator theory and its applications to modern mathematical research. Students will explore infinite-dimensional vector spaces, linear operators, and spectral theory through both theoretical frameworks and computational approaches. The course covers fundamental concepts including Banach and Hilbert spaces, bounded and unbounded operators, compact operators, and spectral decomposition theorems. Students will investigate applications to partial differential equations, quantum mechanics, and optimization theory. Through a combination of theoretical proofs, problem-solving sessions, and computational projects using MATLAB or Python, students will develop expertise in abstract mathematical thinking while gaining practical skills applicable to research in pure mathematics, applied mathematics, physics, and engineering. The course emphasizes connections between functional analysis and other mathematical disciplines, preparing students for advanced research in areas such as harmonic analysis, differential equations, mathematical physics, and numerical analysis. Students will complete a substantial research project applying functional analytic techniques to a problem of their choice, fostering independent research skills essential for doctoral studies or careers in mathematical research and development.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze infinite-dimensional normed spaces and prove fundamental theorems about Banach and Hilbert spaces to establish theoretical foundations for advanced mathematical research
Students will classify linear operators and compute spectral properties through eigenvalue analysis, functional calculus, and spectral decomposition techniques
Students will construct rigorous proofs of major theorems in operator theory by applying techniques from measure theory, topology, and complex analysis
Students will implement numerical algorithms for operator computations using MATLAB or Python to solve concrete problems in differential equations and optimization

# Functional Analysis and Operator Theory
**MATH 571 | 4 Credits | [Semester/Quarter]**

---

## Course Description

This graduate-level course provides a rigorous introduction to functional analysis with emphasis on operator theory and its applications to modern mathematical research. Students will explore infinite-dimensional vector spaces, linear operators, and spectral theory through both theoretical frameworks and computational approaches. The course covers fundamental concepts including Banach and Hilbert spaces, bounded and unbounded operators, compact operators, and spectral decomposition theorems. Students will investigate applications to partial differential equations, quantum mechanics, and optimization theory. Through a combination of theoretical proofs, problem-solving sessions, and computational projects using MATLAB or Python, students will develop expertise in abstract mathematical thinking while gaining practical skills applicable to research in pure mathematics, applied mathematics, physics, and engineering. The course emphasizes connections between functional analysis and other mathematical disciplines, preparing students for advanced research in areas such as harmonic analysis, differential equations, mathematical physics, and numerical analysis. Students will complete a substantial research project applying functional analytic techniques to a problem of their choice, fostering independent research skills essential for doctoral studies or careers in mathematical research and development.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Analyze infinite-dimensional normed spaces and prove fundamental theorems about Banach and Hilbert spaces to establish theoretical foundations for advanced mathematical research  
• Classify linear operators and compute spectral properties through eigenvalue analysis, functional calculus, and spectral decomposition techniques  
• Construct rigorous proofs of major theorems in operator theory by applying techniques from measure theory, topology, and complex analysis  
• Implement numerical algorithms for operator computations using MATLAB or Python to solve concrete problems in differential equations and optimization  

## Target Audience & Prerequisites

**Target Audience:** First or second-year graduate students in mathematics, applied mathematics, or mathematical physics who are pursuing Master's or PhD degrees. This course is essential for students planning research in analysis, partial differential equations, mathematical physics, or related fields requiring advanced analytical techniques.

**Prerequisites:** 
- Completion of graduate-level real analysis (covering Lebesgue integration and metric spaces)
- Advanced linear algebra including finite-dimensional spectral theory
- Undergraduate complex analysis
- Demonstrated proficiency with epsilon-delta proofs and abstract mathematical reasoning
- Familiarity with basic topology and measure theory (strongly recommended)
- Programming experience in MATLAB, Python, or similar computational environment

---

## Required Materials

**Textbooks:**
- *Functional Analysis* by Walter Rudin (Primary text)
- *A Course in Functional Analysis* by John B. Conway (Supplementary)

**Software:**
- MATLAB (available through university license) or Python with NumPy/SciPy
- Access to university computing cluster for computational projects

**Additional Materials:**
- Scientific calculator
- Course materials available on Canvas LMS

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Normed and Metric Spaces
**Topics:** Metric spaces, normed spaces, completeness, Banach spaces  
**Key Concepts:** Cauchy sequences, completeness criterion, norm equivalence  
**Activities:** Problem-solving workshop on metric space topology  

### Week 2: Hilbert Spaces and Orthogonality
**Topics:** Inner product spaces, Hilbert spaces, orthogonal projections  
**Key Concepts:** Parallelogram law, orthogonal complements, projection theorem  
**Assessment:** Quiz 1 - Metric and normed spaces (25 points)  

### Week 3: Linear Operators and Boundedness
**Topics:** Bounded linear operators, operator norms, continuous linear functionals  
**Key Concepts:** Operator norm, uniform boundedness principle  
**Activities:** Computational lab - implementing operator norm calculations  

### Week 4: Fundamental Theorems of Functional Analysis
**Topics:** Hahn-Banach theorem, uniform boundedness principle, open mapping theorem  
**Key Concepts:** Extension of linear functionals, category arguments  
**Assessment:** Problem Set 1 due (50 points)  

### Week 5: Compact Operators and Spectral Theory
**Topics:** Compact operators, Fredholm alternative, spectral theory for compact operators  
**Key Concepts:** Compactness in infinite dimensions, eigenvalue accumulation  
**Activities:Optimizing Multi-Variable Business Functions with Lagrange Multipliers** - Apply functional analytic optimization techniques to constrained problems (150 minutes)  

### Week 6: Spectral Theory of Self-Adjoint Operators
**Topics:** Self-adjoint operators, spectral theorem, functional calculus  
**Key Concepts:** Spectrum, resolvent, spectral measures  
**Assessment:** Midterm Exam (100 points)  

### Week 7: Applications to Differential Equations
**Topics:** Sturm-Liouville problems, Green's functions, solvability conditions  
**Key Concepts:** Boundary value problems, eigenfunction expansions  
**Activities:Engineering a Sustainable City Water Distribution System Using Linear Programming** - Apply operator theory to optimization problems in engineering contexts (115 minutes)  

### Week 8: Unbounded Operators and Semigroups
**Topics:** Unbounded operators, domains, closability, semigroup theory  
**Key Concepts:** Graph norms, generator properties, evolution equations  
**Assessment:** Problem Set 2 due (50 points)  

### Week 9: Applications to Quantum Mechanics and PDEs
**Topics:** Schrödinger operators, heat equation, wave equation  
**Key Concepts:** Self-adjointness, unitary groups, Stone's theorem  
**Activities:Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Emergency Response Networks** - Synthesize functional analysis with real-world optimization (4 hours, project work)  

### Week 10: Advanced Topics and Research Presentations
**Topics:** Current research directions, student project presentations  
**Assessment:** Final Research Project presentations (100 points)  
**Assessment:** Final Comprehensive Exam (100 points)

# Real Analysis I
**Course Syllabus - Fall 2024**

---

## Course Description

This foundational course in real analysis introduces students to the rigorous theoretical underpinnings of calculus and mathematical analysis. Students will explore the structure of real numbers, sequences, series, limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration from a proof-based perspective. The course emphasizes developing mathematical maturity through constructing formal proofs and understanding abstract mathematical concepts. Topics include the completeness axiom, convergence of sequences and series, uniform convergence, properties of continuous functions on closed intervals, the mean value theorem, and the fundamental theorem of calculus with rigorous proofs. Students will learn to write clear, logically sound mathematical arguments and develop critical thinking skills essential for advanced mathematics. This course serves as a bridge between computational mathematics and abstract mathematical theory, preparing students for graduate study in mathematics, careers in mathematical research, actuarial science, or fields requiring strong analytical reasoning skills.

## Learning Objectives

By the completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Construct rigorous epsilon-delta proofs** to demonstrate understanding of limits, continuity, and differentiability in real analysis  
• **Analyze convergence properties** of sequences and series through formal proof techniques including comparison tests, ratio tests, and root tests  
• **Evaluate the completeness** of the real number system by proving fundamental theorems such as the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem and intermediate value theorem  
• **Apply advanced proof methods** using mathematical software like LaTeX to typeset formal mathematical arguments and communicate complex theoretical concepts

## Target Audience

Mathematics majors in their sophomore or junior year who have completed the calculus sequence and are preparing for advanced undergraduate or graduate-level mathematics courses. Also suitable for physics, engineering, or computer science students seeking rigorous mathematical foundations for theoretical work or graduate study.

---

## Required Materials

**Textbook:** *Introduction to Real Analysis* by Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert (4th Edition)  
**Supplementary Text:** *Understanding Analysis* by Stephen Abbott (2nd Edition)  
**Software:** LaTeX distribution (MiKTeX or TeXLive) for typesetting mathematical proofs  
**Hardware:** Graphing calculator (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)  
**Online Platform:** Canvas LMS for assignments and course materials

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: The Real Number System
**Topics:** Axioms of real numbers, ordered fields, completeness axiom, Archimedean property  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 1.1-1.3  
**Activities:** Proof construction workshop on field axioms

### Week 2: Sequences and Convergence
**Topics:** Definition of sequences, limits of sequences, epsilon-N proofs  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 2.1-2.2  
**Activities:** *Optimization in Real Estate Development* (140 min) - applying epsilon-delta techniques to optimization problems  
**Assessment:** Quiz 1 - Basic proof techniques

### Week 3: Properties of Convergent Sequences
**Topics:** Uniqueness of limits, bounded sequences, squeeze theorem  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 2.3-2.4  
**Activities:** Proof writing exercises using LaTeX

### Week 4: Monotone Sequences and Subsequences
**Topics:** Monotone convergence theorem, Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 2.5-2.6  
**Activities:** *Design and Build a Mathematical Model for Optimal Resource Distribution* (120 min) - exploring convergence in optimization contexts

### Week 5: Cauchy Sequences and Completeness
**Topics:** Cauchy criterion, completeness of real numbers  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 2.7  
**Assessment:Advanced Mathematical Reasoning Forum** begins (ongoing discussion)

### Week 6: Introduction to Series
**Topics:** Convergence of infinite series, Cauchy criterion for series  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 3.1-3.2  
**Activities:** Series convergence investigation project

### Week 7: Tests for Convergence
**Topics:** Comparison tests, ratio test, root test, integral test  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 3.3-3.4  
**Activities:** *Optimization in Agricultural Resource Allocation* (90 min) - applying series concepts to modeling

### Week 8: Absolute and Conditional Convergence
**Topics:** Absolute convergence, alternating series test, rearrangements  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 3.5-3.6  
**Assessment:Midterm Exam**

### Week 9: Limits of Functions
**Topics:** Limit of a function at a point, epsilon-delta definition  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 4.1-4.2  
**Activities:** Advanced epsilon-delta proof construction workshop

### Week 10: Continuity
**Topics:** Continuous functions, properties of continuous functions  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 4.3-4.4  
**Activities:** *Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Urban Traffic Flow* (315 min over multiple sessions) - applying continuity concepts

### Week 11: Properties of Continuous Functions on Intervals
**Topics:** Intermediate Value Theorem, Extreme Value Theorem, uniform continuity  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 4.5-4.6  
**Assessment:** Quiz 2 - Continuity and limits

### Week 12: The Derivative
**Topics:** Definition of derivative, differentiation rules from first principles  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 5.1-5.2  
**Activities:** Rigorous proof construction for differentiation theorems

### Week 13: Mean Value Theorem and Applications
**Topics:** Rolle's theorem, Mean Value Theorem, L'Hôpital's rule proof  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 5.3-5.4  
**Activities:** *Optimizing Warehouse Layout Using Linear Programming* (100 min) - connecting analysis to optimization

### Week 14: The Riemann Integral
**Topics:** Riemann sums, definition of Riemann integral, integrability conditions  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 6.1-6.2  
**Assessment:Advanced Mathematical Modeling Portfolio** - Project 2 due

### Week 15: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
**Topics:** FTC Parts I and II with rigorous proofs, applications  
**Readings:** Bartle & Sherbert Ch. 6.3-6.4  
**Activities:** Comprehensive proof presentation preparation

### Week 16: Review and Final Projects
**Topics:** Course synthesis, advanced topics preview  
**Assessment:Advanced Mathematical Modeling Portfolio** - Final submission  
**Assessment:Final Exam**

The course emphasizes developing mathematical reasoning skills while building practical competency in solving systems of linear equations, performing matrix operations, and understanding geometric interpretations of linear algebraic concepts.

# Advanced Topics in Functional Analysis and Operator Theory
**Mathematics 8950 | Spring 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## Course Description

This advanced graduate course explores the theoretical foundations and applications of functional analysis with emphasis on operator theory in infinite-dimensional spaces. Students will investigate the spectral theory of linear operators, compact and bounded operators on Banach and Hilbert spaces, and their applications to partial differential equations and quantum mechanics. The course covers advanced topics including the theory of C*-algebras, unbounded operators, and semigroup theory. Through rigorous proof-based assignments and research projects, students will develop expertise in abstract mathematical reasoning while connecting theoretical concepts to applications in mathematical physics, signal processing, and numerical analysis. This course is essential for students pursuing research in pure mathematics, mathematical physics, or applied mathematics areas requiring sophisticated analytical tools. Students will engage with current research literature and complete an independent project investigating recent developments in operator theory or its applications to emerging fields such as quantum information theory or machine learning.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Analyze spectral properties of bounded and unbounded operators to solve problems in quantum mechanics and partial differential equations  
• Construct rigorous proofs of fundamental theorems in functional analysis through systematic application of topological and algebraic methods  
• Evaluate the structure and properties of C*-algebras and von Neumann algebras by investigating their representation theory and classification schemes  
• Synthesize operator theory techniques using computational tools such as MATLAB or Python to model infinite-dimensional dynamical systems  

---

## Target Audience & Prerequisites

**Target Audience:** Second or third-year PhD students in mathematics, mathematical physics, or related fields who have completed core graduate sequences and are preparing for doctoral research. Ideal for students interested in pure mathematics research areas including functional analysis, operator algebras, or mathematical physics, as well as those pursuing applied research requiring advanced analytical techniques.

**Prerequisites:** Completion of graduate-level real analysis (measure theory, Lebesgue integration), complex analysis, and introductory functional analysis covering normed spaces, Banach and Hilbert spaces, and basic operator theory. Strong background in linear algebra and topology required. Prior exposure to partial differential equations and mathematical physics recommended but not mandatory.

---

## Required Materials

**Textbooks:**
- Conway, J.B. *A Course in Functional Analysis*, 2nd Edition, Springer
- Reed, M. & Simon, B. *Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I: Functional Analysis*, Academic Press
- Kadison, R.V. & Ringrose, J.R. *Fundamentals of the Theory of Operator Algebras*, Volume I, Academic Press

**Software:**
- MATLAB (university license available) or Python with NumPy/SciPy
- LaTeX for typesetting assignments and final project

**Supplementary Resources:**
- Research articles from Journal of Functional Analysis, Advances in Mathematics (provided via course website)
- Online lectures from Abel Prize winners and Fields Medalists (links provided)

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations and Spectral Theory Review
**Module Focus:** Review of Banach and Hilbert spaces, bounded linear operators  
**Key Concepts:** Operator norms, adjoint operators, compact operators  
**Activities:** Problem set on spectral radius calculations  

### Week 2: Spectral Theory of Bounded Operators
**Module Focus:** Spectrum, resolvent, spectral radius theorem  
**Key Concepts:** Point spectrum, continuous spectrum, residual spectrum  
**Assessment:** Real-World Problem Solving Discussion (100 points)  

### Week 3: Compact Operators and Fredholm Theory
**Module Focus:** Properties of compact operators, Fredholm alternative  
**Key Concepts:** Riesz-Schauder theory, index theory  
**Activities:** Optimization of Urban Water Distribution Networks (120 minutes)  

### Week 4: Self-Adjoint Operators and Spectral Theorem
**Module Focus:** Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators  
**Key Concepts:** Eigenvalue decomposition, spectral measures  
**Activities:** Design and Construct Dynamic Optimization System (Week 1 of 5)  

### Week 5: Unbounded Operators - Fundamentals
**Module Focus:** Closed operators, domains, extensions  
**Key Concepts:** Graph topology, closable operators, self-adjoint extensions  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 2)  

### Week 6: Unbounded Self-Adjoint Operators
**Module Focus:** Spectral theorem for unbounded self-adjoint operators  
**Key Concepts:** Spectral families, Stone's theorem  
**Assessment:** Advanced Calculus and Linear Algebra Integration Exam (100 points)  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 3)  

### Week 7: Applications to Quantum Mechanics
**Module Focus:** Quantum mechanical operators, momentum and position  
**Key Concepts:** Heisenberg uncertainty principle, canonical commutation relations  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 4)  

### Week 8: Introduction to C*-Algebras
**Module Focus:** Definition, examples, basic properties  
**Key Concepts:** Involution, C*-identity, Gelfand-Naimark theorem  
**Assessment:** Statistical Analysis Laboratory Report Due (100 points)  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 5 - Final presentations)  

### Week 9: Representation Theory of C*-Algebras
**Module Focus:** *-representations, irreducible representations  
**Key Concepts:** GNS construction, pure states  
**Activities:** Optimization of Urban Traffic Flow (130 minutes)  

### Week 10: Von Neumann Algebras
**Module Focus:** Weak and strong operator topologies, double commutant theorem  
**Key Concepts:** Type classification, factors  
**Activities:** Design Mathematical Urban Planning Model (105 minutes)  

### Week 11: Semigroup Theory - Fundamentals
**Module Focus:** One-parameter semigroups, generators  
**Key Concepts:** Hille-Yosida theorem, contraction semigroups  

### Week 12: Applications of Semigroup Theory
**Module Focus:** Evolution equations, heat equation, wave equation  
**Key Concepts:** Analytic semigroups, interpolation spaces  
**Activities:** Predictive Financial Model Construction (4.5 hours)  

### Week 13: Advanced Topics - Quantum Information Theory
**Module Focus:** Quantum channels, completely positive maps  
**Key Concepts:** Stinespring dilation, Kraus representation  

### Week 14: Research Project Presentations I
**Student presentations of independent research projectsAssessment:** Real-World Mathematics Portfolio Due (100 points)  

### Week 15: Research Project Presentations II  
**Student presentations continuedAssessment:** Personal Budget Planning Project Due (100 points)

**Comprehensive written reports on independent research projects**

# Linear Algebra and Matrix Theory

---

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra, focusing on vector spaces, linear transformations, and matrix theory with applications across science, engineering, and data science. Students will explore fundamental concepts including systems of linear equations, matrix operations, determinants, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and computational proficiency, preparing students to apply linear algebraic methods to real-world problems in computer graphics, machine learning, optimization, and engineering systems. 

Through a combination of rigorous proofs, computational exercises, and practical applications, students will develop the mathematical maturity necessary for advanced coursework in mathematics, statistics, computer science, and related fields. The course integrates technology tools including MATLAB or Python for matrix computations and visualization. Topics covered include Gaussian elimination, vector spaces and subspaces, linear independence and basis, orthogonality and least squares, diagonalization, and singular value decomposition. Students will complete projects that demonstrate the power of linear algebra in modeling and solving contemporary problems in data analysis, image processing, and scientific computing.

# Linear Algebra and Its Applications
**MATH 3310 | 3 Credit Hours | Spring 2024**

---

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra with emphasis on both theoretical foundations and practical applications across multiple disciplines. Students will explore vector spaces, linear transformations, matrix operations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and systems of linear equations. The course bridges abstract mathematical concepts with real-world applications in computer science, engineering, economics, and data science. Through a combination of rigorous proofs and computational problem-solving, students develop critical thinking skills essential for advanced mathematics and quantitative fields. Topics include Gaussian elimination, determinants, orthogonality, diagonalization, and least squares approximation. Students will use mathematical software to visualize concepts and solve complex problems, preparing them for advanced coursework in differential equations, numerical analysis, optimization, and machine learning. The course emphasizes both hand calculations and computational approaches, ensuring students understand underlying principles while gaining practical skills for modern applications.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Analyze** vector spaces and linear transformations to model real-world phenomena in engineering and computer graphics applications  
• **Solve** systems of linear equations and optimization problems through matrix operations and computational software like MATLAB or Python  
• **Evaluate** eigenvalues and eigenvectors by applying diagonalization techniques to problems in data analysis and dynamical systems  
• **Construct** mathematical proofs and verify linear algebra concepts using both analytical methods and computer algebra systems  

## Target Audience

This course is designed for second or third-year undergraduate students majoring in mathematics, engineering, computer science, physics, or economics who seek to develop strong analytical and computational skills. Ideal for students planning to pursue advanced coursework in applied mathematics, data science, machine learning, or graduate studies in STEM fields.

**MATH 8XX • Quarter System • 4 Credits**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Schedule:** [Days] [Time] in [Room]  
**Final Exam:** [Date and Time] in [Room]  

**Course Website:** [LMS/Website URL]  
**Prerequisites:** Completion of undergraduate real analysis, abstract algebra, and point-set topology. Graduate-level algebraic topology covering fundamental groups, covering spaces, homology theory, and cohomology theory. Familiarity with category theory and basic homological algebra including exact sequences, chain complexes, and derived functors. Mathematical maturity equivalent to passing graduate qualifying examinations in analysis and algebra.

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This graduate-level course explores advanced concepts in algebraic topology, focusing on spectral sequences, characteristic classes, and modern computational methods. Students will develop expertise in homological algebra techniques applied to topological problems, including the construction and application of Serre and Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequences. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical applications in geometric topology, differential geometry, and mathematical physics. Students will engage with current research literature and learn to apply sophisticated topological invariants to classify spaces and maps. Topics include fiber bundles, vector bundles, Chern classes, Stiefel-Whitney classes, and cobordism theory. The curriculum integrates traditional proof-based approaches with modern computational topology tools, preparing students for research in pure mathematics, theoretical physics, or data science applications. Through rigorous problem-solving and independent research projects, students will develop the mathematical maturity necessary for doctoral research or advanced positions in academia and industry.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Construct and analyze spectral sequences** to compute homology and cohomology groups of complex topological spaces in algebraic topology research contexts
• **Evaluate characteristic classes** of vector bundles through explicit calculations using Chern-Weil theory and cohomological methods
• **Prove fundamental theorems** in fiber bundle theory by applying advanced techniques from homological algebra and differential geometry
• **Implement computational topology algorithms** using Python and SageMath to verify theoretical results and explore conjectures in modern research problems

## TARGET AUDIENCE

Graduate students in mathematics, mathematical physics, or related fields who have completed foundational courses in algebraic topology and seek advanced research preparation.
