# Neural Networks for Real-Time Computer Vision Applications
**Course Code:** CS 4XX | **Credits:** 3 | **Semester:** Fall/Spring 2024

## Course Description

This hands-on course bridges the gap between theoretical neural network concepts and practical computer vision implementation. Students will design, train, and deploy convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for real-world applications including autonomous vehicle perception, medical image analysis, and augmented reality systems. The curriculum emphasizes optimization techniques for real-time performance, covering edge computing deployment, model compression, and hardware acceleration using GPUs and specialized AI chips. Through project-based learning, students will work with industry-standard frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, implementing solutions for object detection, image segmentation, and facial recognition systems. The course includes partnerships with local tech companies, providing students opportunities to work on live computer vision challenges. Students will learn to handle large-scale image datasets, implement transfer learning strategies, and address ethical considerations in AI-powered vision systems. By semester's end, each student will have developed a complete computer vision pipeline from data preprocessing to model deployment, gaining practical experience in MLOps practices and cloud-based AI services for scalable computer vision solutions.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
• Design and implement convolutional neural networks optimized for real-time computer vision tasks
• Deploy AI models on edge devices and cloud platforms using modern MLOPs practices
• Evaluate and address ethical implications of computer vision systems in society

## Required Materials

- **Textbooks:** 
  - *Deep Learning* by Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville
  - *Hands-On Computer Vision with TensorFlow 2* by Benjamin Planche and Eliot Andres
- **Software:** Python 3.8+, TensorFlow 2.x, PyTorch, OpenCV, Jupyter Notebooks
- **Hardware:** Personal laptop with minimum 8GB RAM (GPU recommended but not required)
- **Cloud Access:** AWS/Google Cloud credits provided for model training

# Enterprise Software Architecture and DevOps Integration Capstone
**Course Syllabus - Spring 2024**

---

## Course Description

This capstone course challenges senior computer science students to design, architect, and deploy enterprise-grade software systems while implementing comprehensive DevOps pipelines. Students work in cross-functional teams to tackle real-world problems provided by industry partners, focusing on scalable microservices architecture, containerization, continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD), and cloud-native solutions. The course emphasizes the complete software development lifecycle, from requirements gathering and system design to production deployment and monitoring. Students must demonstrate proficiency in modern architectural patterns, infrastructure as code, automated testing strategies, and production-ready deployment practices. Each team delivers a fully functional enterprise application with proper documentation, monitoring dashboards, and automated deployment pipelines. The capstone project requires integration of multiple technologies including container orchestration platforms, cloud services, monitoring tools, and security implementations. Students present their solutions to industry professionals and demonstrate their systems under realistic load conditions. This course bridges the gap between academic learning and professional software engineering practices, preparing graduates for senior developer and DevOps engineering roles in modern technology organizations.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement scalable microservices architectures using industry-standard patterns and best practices  
• Create comprehensive CI/CD pipelines with automated testing, security scanning, and deployment strategies  
• Demonstrate expertise in containerization, orchestration, and cloud-native application development  
• Apply enterprise-level monitoring, logging, and observability practices to production systems  
• Collaborate effectively in cross-functional teams while managing complex software engineering projects  

---

## Weekly Schedule

### **Week 1-2: Foundation and Algorithm Optimization ReviewModule:** Big O Notation and Algorithm Complexity Analysis
- **Concepts:**
  - Big O Notation: Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity: Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size
- **Activities:** Programming Language Syntax Element Identification Challenge (45 min)
- **Focus:** Review algorithmic thinking essential for enterprise system optimization

### **Week 3-4: Data Structure Optimization for Enterprise SystemsModule:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- **Concepts:**
  - Binary Search Tree Property: Left subtree contains values less than parent, right subtree contains values greater than parent
  - Tree Traversal Algorithms: In-order, pre-order, and post-order traversal methods for visiting all nodes systematically
- **Activities:** Python Data Types Memory Card Challenge (30 min)
- **Focus:** Apply efficient data structures in microservices design

### **Week 5-6: Distributed System Data ManagementModule:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Collision Resolution
- **Concepts:**
  - Hash Function: A function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
  - Collision Resolution: Techniques to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
- **Activities:** Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recall Challenge (45 min)
- **Focus:** Implement distributed caching and data partitioning strategies

### **Week 7-8: Network Architecture and Service DiscoveryModule:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
- **Concepts:**
  - Graph Representation: Adjacency lists and adjacency matrices for storing graph data structures
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS): Level-order traversal using queues to explore graphs systematically
- **Activities:** Computer System Components Memory Match and Label (35 min)
- **Focus:** Design service mesh architectures and network topology optimization

### **Week 9-10: Microservices Architecture Implementation**
- **Focus:** Containerization with Docker, Kubernetes orchestration
- **Activities:** Programming Language Syntax Memory Card Challenge (45 min)
- **Deliverable:** Microservices architecture design document

### **Week 11-12: CI/CD Pipeline Development**
- **Focus:** Jenkins, GitLab CI, automated testing frameworks
- **Activities:** Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge (45 min)
- **Deliverable:** Automated deployment pipeline implementation

### **Week 13-14: Cloud Integration and Monitoring**
- **Focus:** AWS/Azure/GCP services, Prometheus, Grafana, ELK stack
- **Activities:** Programming Language Syntax Matching Challenge (45 min)
- **Deliverable:** Production monitoring and alerting system

### **Week 15-16: Final Integration and Presentations**
- **Focus:** Load testing, security auditing, final system integration
- **Activities:** Binary Number System Flashcard Recall Challenge (45 min)
- **Deliverable:** Industry presentation and system demonstration

---

# Bayesian Modeling and Uncertainty Quantification in Modern Data Systems

**Course Code:** DS 495  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** Statistics (STAT 301), Linear Algebra (MATH 251), Programming in Python (CS 201)  
**Meeting Time:** Tuesday/Thursday 2:00-3:50 PM  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

## Instructor Information

## Course Description

This advanced course explores the critical role of uncertainty quantification in data science through the lens of Bayesian statistical methodology. Students will delve into hierarchical modeling, Monte Carlo methods, and probabilistic programming to address real-world problems where uncertainty is inherent and must be rigorously quantified. The course emphasizes the transition from frequentist to Bayesian thinking, covering advanced topics including variational inference, Gaussian processes, and Bayesian neural networks. Through hands-on projects with complex, messy datasets from domains like climate science, finance, and healthcare, students will learn to build models that not only make predictions but also communicate the confidence and uncertainty in those predictions. Special attention is given to computational challenges, including MCMC diagnostics, model comparison using information criteria, and scalable approximate inference methods. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to tackle high-stakes data science problems where understanding and communicating uncertainty is as important as point estimates, preparing them for roles in research, risk assessment, and decision-making under uncertainty.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master Bayesian Inference Techniques**: Students will master Bayesian inference techniques including MCMC sampling, variational inference, and probabilistic programming using tools like Stan and PyMC

2. **Apply Advanced Modeling Techniques**: Students will apply hierarchical modeling and Gaussian processes to complex, multi-level data structures with appropriate uncertainty quantification

3. **Develop Model Validation Expertise**: Students will develop expertise in model criticism, comparison, and validation within the Bayesian framework for high-stakes decision making

## Required Materials

- **Textbook:** McElreath, R. (2020). *Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan*, 2nd Edition
- **Software:** Python 3.8+, PyMC, Stan, Jupyter Notebooks
- **Computing:** Personal laptop with minimum 8GB RAM recommended
- **Additional Resources:** Course materials and datasets available on course website

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation and Data Understanding
**Topic:** Course Introduction and Data Exploration Fundamentals

**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization Fundamentals
- Univariate Analysis: Statistical summaries, distributions, and visualizations for single variables including histograms, box plots, and density plots
- Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis: Correlation matrices, scatter plots, pair plots, and heatmaps to explore relationships between variables

**Activities:**
- Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Customer Data (60 minutes)
- Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Performance Analysis (45 minutes)

### Week 2: Data Preparation for Bayesian Analysis
**Topic:** Feature Engineering with Uncertainty Considerations

**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning
- Feature scaling and normalization - techniques like StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler to ensure features are on comparable scales
- Categorical encoding methods - one-hot encoding, label encoding, target encoding, and binary encoding for handling categorical variables

**Activities:**
- Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Purchase Data Analysis (60 minutes)

### Week 3: Introduction to Bayesian Thinking
**Topic:** From Frequentist to Bayesian Paradigm
- Bayes' theorem and its implications
- Prior distributions and their selection
- Posterior inference basics

### Week 4: Probabilistic Programming Fundamentals
**Topic:** Introduction to PyMC and Stan
- Basic model specification
- Simple conjugate models
- Introduction to MCMC sampling

**Activities:**
- Interpreting Bias-Variance Trade-off Through Cross-Validation Learning Curves (75 minutes)

### Week 5: Monte Carlo Methods I
**Topic:** Markov Chain Monte Carlo Fundamentals
- Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
- Gibbs sampling
- Convergence diagnostics

### Week 6: Monte Carlo Methods II
**Topic:** Advanced MCMC Techniques
- Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
- No U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)
- MCMC diagnostics and troubleshooting

**Activities:**
- Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Ensemble Methods (80 minutes)

### Week 7: Hierarchical Models I
**Topic:** Multi-level Data Structures
- Partial pooling concepts
- Random effects models
- Shrinkage and regularization

### Week 8: Hierarchical Models II
**Topic:** Complex Hierarchical Structures
- Varying intercepts and slopes
- Cross-classified models
- Model comparison techniques

**Activities:**
- Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models for Customer Churn Prediction (80 minutes)

### Week 9: Model Comparison and Selection
**Topic:** Bayesian Model Selection
- Information criteria (WAIC, LOO-CV)
- Bayes factors
- Model averaging

### Week 10: Variational Inference
**Topic:** Scalable Approximate Inference
- Variational Bayes fundamentals
- Automatic Differentiation Variational Inference (ADVI)
- When to use VI vs. MCMC

**Activities:**
- Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Satisfaction Analysis (50 minutes)

### Week 11: Gaussian Processes
**Topic:** Non-parametric Bayesian Methods
- GP fundamentals and kernel functions
- GP regression and classification
- Hyperparameter inference

### Week 12: Bayesian Neural Networks
**Topic:** Deep Learning with Uncertainty
- Bayesian interpretation of neural networks
- Variational dropout and uncertainty
- Practical implementation strategies

### Week 13: Advanced Applications I
**Topic:** Time Series and Temporal Models
- State space models
- Dynamic linear models
- Forecasting with uncertainty

**Activities:**
- Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Predicting Customer Churn Using Industry-Standard Metrics (180 minutes)

### Week 14: Advanced Applications II
**Topic:** Specialized Domains
- Survival analysis
- Spatial models
- Missing data imputation

### Week 15: Final Projects and Presentations
**Topic:** Student Project Presentations and Course Wrap-up
- Project presentations
- Real-world case studies
- Career applications and next steps

**Activities:**
- Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Fraud Detection (3.5 hours)

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment | Type | Points | Due Date |
|------------|------|---------|----------|
| Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Project | Project | 100 | Week 8 |
| Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Lab Report | Lab Report | 100 | Week 9 |
| Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Assessment: Model Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization | Quiz | 100 | Week 10 |
| Ethical AI and Algorithmic Bias in Production Systems: A Critical Analysis Discussion | Discussion | 100 | Week 12 |
| Data Science Process and Insights Presentation | Presentation | 100 | Week 15 |

**Total Points:** 500

### Grading Scale
- A: 450-500 points (90-100%)
- B: 400-449 points (80-89%)
- C: 350-399 points (70-79%)
- D: 300-349 points (60-69%)
- F: Below 300 points (<60%)

## Assessment Details

### Major Project (200 points total)
The Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Project and accompanying lab report form the core assessment of your Bayesian modeling skills. You will work with a real-world dataset to build hierarchical Bayesian models that not only predict customer churn but also quantify the uncertainty in these predictions.

### Presentations (100 points)
Your final presentation should demonstrate mastery of Bayesian concepts applied to a domain-specific problem, with emphasis on uncertainty communication and model interpretation.

### Quiz (100 points)
The quiz will assess your understanding of model selection, hyperparameter optimization, and computational considerations in Bayesian modeling.

### Discussion (100 points)

course_info.title: Extracting Gold from Digital Noise: Advanced Pattern Mining in Massive Datasets
course_info.description: This intensive course transforms students into digital archaeologists, equipped to excavate valuable insights from massive, chaotic datasets. Students will master cutting-edge pattern mining algorithms including frequent itemset mining, sequential pattern discovery, and graph mining techniques. Through hands-on projects involving real-world datasets from social media, e-commerce, and IoT sensors, students will learn to identify hidden associations, temporal patterns, and anomalies that traditional analytics miss. The course emphasizes computational efficiency, scalability challenges, and the art of distinguishing signal from noise in big data environments. Students will implement mining algorithms from scratch, optimize them for distributed computing platforms, and develop novel approaches to emerging mining problems. Weekly hackathons simulate industry pressure, where teams compete to extract the most valuable insights from increasingly complex datasets. By semester's end, students will have built a portfolio of mining solutions addressing real business problems, from recommendation systems to fraud detection networks.

Students will design and deploy scalable mining solutions using distributed computing frameworks to handle terabyte-scale data processing challenges
Students will develop expertise in anomaly detection and rare pattern discovery techniques for applications in fraud detection, cybersecurity, and quality control systems

# EXTRACTING GOLD FROM DIGITAL NOISE: ADVANCED PATTERN MINING IN MASSIVE DATASETS
**Course Code:** CS 485 | **Credits:** 3 | **Prerequisites:** Data Structures & Algorithms, Statistics, Python Programming

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Meeting:** [Days/Times] in [Room Location]  
**Semester:** [Term Year]

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This intensive course transforms students into digital archaeologists, equipped to excavate valuable insights from massive, chaotic datasets. Students will master cutting-edge pattern mining algorithms including frequent itemset mining, sequential pattern discovery, and graph mining techniques. Through hands-on projects involving real-world datasets from social media, e-commerce, and IoT sensors, students will learn to identify hidden associations, temporal patterns, and anomalies that traditional analytics miss. The course emphasizes computational efficiency, scalability challenges, and the art of distinguishing signal from noise in big data environments. Students will implement mining algorithms from scratch, optimize them for distributed computing platforms, and develop novel approaches to emerging mining problems. Weekly hackathons simulate industry pressure, where teams compete to extract the most valuable insights from increasingly complex datasets. By semester's end, students will have built a portfolio of mining solutions addressing real business problems, from recommendation systems to fraud detection networks.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Implement and optimize advanced pattern mining algorithms** for frequent itemsets, sequential patterns, and graph structures in massive datasets
• **Design and deploy scalable mining solutions** using distributed computing frameworks to handle terabyte-scale data processing challenges  
• **Develop expertise in anomaly detection and rare pattern discovery techniques** for applications in fraud detection, cybersecurity, and quality control systems

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

- **Textbook:** *Pattern Mining: Algorithms and Applications* (recommended)
- **Software:** Python 3.8+, Apache Spark, Jupyter Notebooks, Git
- **Hardware:** Laptop capable of running virtual machines (8GB RAM minimum)
- **Platform Access:** AWS Academic Credits (provided), course GitHub repository

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Foundations of Pattern Mining
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization
- **Concepts:**
  - Statistical summaries: descriptive statistics including measures of central tendency, dispersion, skewness, and kurtosis to characterize data distributions
  - Data profiling: systematic examination of data types, missing values, duplicate records, and data quality assessment techniques

### Week 2: Advanced EDA with Python
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Python

  - Data profiling - systematic examination of dataset structure, completeness, and quality metrics
  - Statistical visualization - graphical representation of data distributions, relationships, and patterns using appropriate chart types

### Week 3: Feature Engineering Foundations
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts:**
  - Feature encoding - Converting categorical variables to numerical format using one-hot encoding, label encoding, and target encoding
  - Feature scaling and normalization - Standardizing numerical features using min-max scaling, z-score normalization, and robust scaling techniques
- **Activity:** Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Performance Dashboard (45 min)

### Week 4: Multivariate Analysis & Relationships
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization

# Predictive Modeling in Real-World Business Scenarios
**Course Code:** DS 350 | **Credits:** 3 | **Semester:** Spring 2024

---

## Course Description

This hands-on course immerses students in the complete lifecycle of building predictive models for authentic business challenges. Students work with real datasets from partner organizations to develop models that address problems like customer churn prediction, demand forecasting, fraud detection, and price optimization. The course emphasizes model selection, feature engineering, validation strategies, and deployment considerations rather than theoretical foundations. Students learn to navigate messy data, handle class imbalance, incorporate domain expertise, and communicate model insights to non-technical stakeholders. Through semester-long projects with industry mentors, students experience the iterative nature of model development, including failed experiments and model refinement. The curriculum covers ensemble methods, time series forecasting, recommendation systems, and A/B testing for model evaluation. Students also explore model interpretability, ethical considerations, and the business impact of modeling decisions. By semester's end, students will have built a portfolio of deployed models and gained practical experience in translating business requirements into modeling solutions. The course culminates in presentations to industry partners, providing students with real-world feedback on their modeling approaches and business recommendations.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design and implement** end-to-end predictive modeling pipelines for complex business problems using industry-standard tools and methodologies
• **Evaluate and select** appropriate modeling techniques based on business constraints, data characteristics, and performance requirements in real-world scenarios
• **Develop expertise** in feature engineering, model validation, and deployment strategies while working with authentic datasets from industry partners
• **Demonstrate proficiency** in communicating model results, limitations, and business implications to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
• **Apply ethical modeling practices** and assess the broader impact of predictive models on business decisions and society

---

## Prerequisites

- DS 250: Introduction to Machine Learning
- STAT 260: Applied Statistics
- CS 150: Programming in Python
- MATH 220: Linear Algebra

---

## Required Materials

**Textbooks:**
- *Hands-On Machine Learning* by Aurélien Géron (3rd Edition)
- *Feature Engineering for Machine Learning* by Alice Zheng & Amanda Casari

**Software:**
- Python 3.8+ with Anaconda distribution
- Jupyter Notebooks
- Access to cloud computing platform (provided)

**Hardware:**
- Laptop capable of running Python and Jupyter Notebooks

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation and Data Understanding
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization with Python
- **Concepts:**
  - Univariate analysis - Statistical examination of individual variables including distribution analysis, measures of central tendency, and variability assessment
  - Bivariate and multivariate analysis - Exploration of relationships between multiple variables using correlation matrices, scatter plots, and contingency tables
- **Activities:**
  - Evaluating Data Quality and Visualization Effectiveness in Real-World Datasets (60 min)
- **Deliverables:** Industry partner dataset assignments distributed

### Week 2: Data Quality and Visualization
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization Fundamentals  
- **Concepts:**
  - Univariate Analysis - examining individual variables through measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape using histograms, box plots, and summary statistics
  - Bivariate Analysis - exploring relationships between two variables using correlation coefficients, scatter plots, and cross-tabulations to identify patterns and dependencies
- **Activities:**
  - Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making (70 min)

### Week 3: Advanced EDA and Pattern Recognition
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization
- **Concepts:**
  - Descriptive Statistics - measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape for understanding data characteristics
  - Data Quality Assessment - systematic evaluation of completeness, consistency, accuracy, and validity in datasets
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Healthcare Data (60 min)

### Week 4: Feature Engineering Foundations
**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning
- **Concepts:**
  - Feature scaling and normalization - Methods to standardize feature ranges including min-max scaling, z-score normalization, and robust scaling to handle outliers
  - Categorical encoding techniques - Strategies for converting categorical data into numerical format including one-hot encoding, ordinal encoding, and target-based encoding methods
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Estate Data Analysis (85 min)

### Week 5: Advanced Feature Engineering
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts:**
  - Feature transformation - mathematical operations applied to raw variables including scaling, normalization, log transforms, and polynomial features to improve model compatibility
  - Categorical encoding - techniques for converting categorical variables into numerical representations including one-hot encoding, target encoding, and embedding methods
- **Activities:**
  - Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Online Shopping Behavior (45 min)

### Week 6: Feature Creation and Selection
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Predictive Modeling
- **Concepts:**
  - Feature Creation - Generating new variables through mathematical operations, polynomial features, interaction terms, and domain-specific transformations
  - Feature Selection - Statistical and algorithmic methods to identify the most relevant features including filter, wrapper, and embedded approaches
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps for Customer Churn Prediction (45 min)
- **Assessment:** Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Implementation and Analysis Quiz (Due)

### Week 7: Model Selection and Validation
**Focus:** Business problem formulation and baseline model development
- **Topics:**
  - Translating business requirements into modeling problems
  - Baseline model establishment
  - Cross-validation strategies for business scenarios
- **Project Milestone:** Problem definition and baseline model (Industry mentor meetings begin)

### Week 8: Ensemble Methods and Model Complexity
**Focus:** Advanced modeling techniques for business applications
- **Topics:**
  - Random forests, gradient boosting, and stacking
  - Bias-variance tradeoff in business contexts
  - Model complexity vs. interpretability
- **Activities:**
  - Comparative Analysis of Bias-Variance Tradeoff Across Ensemble Methods Using Bootstrap Sampling Distributions (105 min)

### Week 9: Model Interpretability and Feature Importance
**Focus:** Understanding and explaining model decisions
- **Topics:**
  - SHAP values and LIME
  - Feature importance in ensemble methods
  - Model interpretability for stakeholders
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Feature Importance in Gradient Boosting Models for High-Dimensional Healthcare Data (90 min)

### Week 10: Time Series Forecasting
**Focus:** Sequential data and temporal patterns
- **Topics:**
  - Demand forecasting techniques
  - Seasonality and trend analysis
  - ARIMA and Prophet models
- **Assessment:** Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Lab Report (Due)

### Week 11: Recommendation Systems and Personalization
**Focus:** Building recommendation engines for business
- **Topics:**
  - Collaborative filtering and content-based methods
  - Matrix factorization techniques
  - Evaluation metrics for recommendation systems

### Week 12: A/B Testing and Model Evaluation
**Focus:** Testing model performance in production
- **Topics:**
  - Experimental design for model validation
  - Statistical significance in business testing
  - Online vs. offline evaluation metrics
- **Activities:**
  - Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Multiple Business Contexts (120 min)

### Week 13: Ethical AI and Bias Mitigation
**Focus:** Responsible modeling practices
- **Topics:**
  - Algorithmic bias detection and mitigation
  - Fairness metrics and constraints
  - Ethical considerations in deployment
- **Assessment:** Ethical AI Implementation: Critical Analysis of Bias Mitigation Strategies in Production Systems (Due)

### Week 14: Model Deployment and Production Considerations
**Focus:** Transitioning from prototype to production
- **Topics:**
  - Model serving and API development
  - Monitoring and model drift detection
  - Scaling considerations
- **Activities:**
  - Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Prediction Systems (180 min)

### Week 15: Industry Presentations and Portfolio Review
**Focus:** Capstone presentations to industry partners
- **Assessment:** Data Science Project Presentation: Exploring a Real-World Dataset
- **Assessment:** Customer Churn Prediction and Business Impact Analysis (Final Project Due)

### Week 16: Final Examinations Week
**Focus:** Course wrap-up and reflection
- Portfolio submissions and peer evaluations

---

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment Type | Description | Points | Due Date | Weight |
|-----------------|-------------|---------|----------|---------|
| **Quiz** | Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Implementation and Analysis Quiz | 100 | Week 6 | 15% |
| **Lab Report** | Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Lab Report | 100 | Week 10 | 20% |
| **Discussion** | Ethical AI Implementation: Critical Analysis of Bias Mitigation Strategies in Production Systems | 100 | Week 13 | 15% |
| **Presentation** | Data Science Project Presentation: Exploring a Real-World Dataset | 100 | Week 15 | 20% |
| **Final Project** | Customer Churn Prediction and Business Impact Analysis | 100 | Week 15 | 30% |

**Total Points:** 500

### Grading Scale
- A: 90-100% (450-500 points)
- B: 80-89% (400-449 points)  
- C: 70-79% (350-399 points)
- D: 60-69% (300-349 points)
- F: Below 60% (<300 points)

---

## Course Policies

### Attendance Policy
Regular attendance is essential for success in this hands-on course. Students are expected to attend all class sessions. More than two unexcused absences may result in a reduction of the final grade. Industry mentor meetings are mandatory and absences must be communicated 24 hours in advance.

### Late Assignment Policy
- **0-24 hours late:** 10% penalty
- **24-48 hours late:** 20% penalty  
- **48-72 hours late:** 30% penalty
- **More than 72 hours late:** Assignment not accepted without prior arrangement

Extensions may be granted for documented emergencies or health issues with advance notice.

### Technology Policy
Laptops and tablets are required for in-class activities and are expected to be used for course-related work only during class time. Mobile phones should be silenced and put away during class sessions and industry mentor meetings.

### Collaboration and Academic Integrity
- **Encouraged:** Discussion of concepts, sharing of resources, peer review of presentations
- **Prohibited:** Copying code or analysis without attribution, sharing of quiz answers, submitting identical work
- All sources must be properly cited. Industry datasets are confidential and may not be shared outside the course.

### Industry Partnership Guidelines
Students will work with real industry datasets and mentors throughout the semester. Professional conduct is expected in all interactions:
- Maintain confidentiality of proprietary data and business information
- Communicate professionally and respectfully with industry mentors
- Meet all scheduled appointments and deadlines
- Follow data use agreements and security protocols

### Accommodation Statement
Students with documented disabilities who may need accommodations should schedule an appointment with the instructor as soon as possible. All discussions will remain confidential. Students should contact the Office of Disability Services to verify their eligibility for reasonable accommodations.

### Communication Policy
- Check course learning management system regularly for announcements
- Email responses within 24-48 hours on weekdays
- Use appropriate academic communication standards### Professional Development
This course emphasizes real-world skills and industry connections:
- Industry mentors may provide networking opportunities and career guidance
- Students are encouraged to document their projects for professional portfolios
- Course completion certificates will be provided upon successful completion
- Industry partners may offer internship or job opportunities to outstanding students

# PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS AND MODEL DEPLOYMENT: FROM ALGORITHM TO PRODUCTION
**Course Syllabus - Spring 2024**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Course Code:** DSCI 3850  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** DSCI 2100 (Introduction to Data Science), STAT 2010 (Statistics), CSCI 2200 (Programming Fundamentals)  
**Meeting Time:** Tuesday/Thursday 2:00-3:30 PM  

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This comprehensive course bridges the gap between theoretical machine learning and real-world implementation by focusing on the complete predictive analytics pipeline. Students will master the art of transforming raw data into deployed machine learning solutions that drive business decisions. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on experience with end-to-end model development, from feature engineering and algorithm selection to model validation and production deployment. Students will work with diverse datasets across industries, learning to evaluate model performance, handle concept drift, and implement continuous learning systems. The course covers advanced topics including ensemble methods, hyperparameter optimization, model interpretability, and MLOps practices. Special attention is given to ethical considerations, bias detection, and responsible AI deployment. Through industry-partnered projects, students will experience the challenges of scaling models, managing model lifecycles, and communicating insights to stakeholders. By course completion, students will have built and deployed multiple production-ready machine learning systems, gaining practical expertise in cloud platforms, containerization, and automated model monitoring systems essential for modern data science careers.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Pipeline Design & Implementation:** Students will design and implement complete machine learning pipelines from data preprocessing through production deployment
2. **Advanced Model Optimization:** Students will master advanced ensemble methods, hyperparameter tuning, and model optimization techniques for maximum predictive performance
3. **MLOps Proficiency:** Students will develop proficiency in MLOps practices including model versioning, continuous integration, automated testing, and monitoring systems
4. **Ethical AI Implementation:** Students will evaluate and mitigate algorithmic bias while ensuring model interpretability and ethical AI deployment
5. **Cloud Deployment Expertise:** Students will demonstrate expertise in cloud-based model deployment using containerization and API development for scalable solutions

---

### Week 1: Foundation - Data Exploration and Profiling
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis with Python: Unveiling Patterns in Data

- Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis - correlation coefficients, cross-tabulation, and association measures
- **Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis (45 min)

### Week 4: Data Quality and Cleaning Strategies
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Python
- Data profiling - dataset dimensions, data types, missing values, and basic statistics
- Univariate analysis - histograms, box plots, and summary statistics for distribution understanding
- **Activity:** Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for Customer Purchase Dataset (95 min)

### Week 5: Feature Engineering Fundamentals

**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning
- Feature transformation: scaling, normalization, log transforms for improved model convergence
- Categorical encoding: one-hot encoding, target encoding, and embedding methods
- **Activity:** Interpreting Advanced Feature Engineering Transformations in High-Dimensional Customer Churn Prediction (110 min)

### Week 7: Feature Selection and Optimization

- Feature Creation - mathematical transformations, polynomial features, binning, and encoding

# Scalable Computational Frameworks for Massive Dataset Analysis
**CS 485 | Data Science Program | Fall 2024**

---

## Course Description

This advanced theoretical course examines the mathematical foundations and computational paradigms underlying big data processing systems. Students explore distributed computing models, algorithmic complexity in massive-scale environments, and theoretical limits of data processing architectures. The curriculum emphasizes formal analysis of MapReduce paradigms, stream processing algorithms, and parallel computation theories. Through rigorous mathematical frameworks, students investigate trade-offs between computational efficiency, memory constraints, and processing latency in petabyte-scale systems. Key topics include distributed consensus algorithms, fault tolerance mechanisms, data partitioning strategies, and theoretical foundations of NoSQL databases. The course provides deep theoretical understanding of how modern big data systems achieve scalability, examining the mathematical principles behind Apache Spark, Hadoop ecosystems, and cloud-native processing frameworks.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will:

• **Master theoretical principles** governing distributed computing architectures and their application to massive dataset processing challenges

# Behavioral Pattern Mining Laboratory: Extracting Insights from Digital Footprints

**Course Code:** DSCI 3850  
**Credits:** 3 credit hours

**Meeting Time:** Tuesday/Thursday 2:00-3:50 PM

## Course Description

This hands-on laboratory course focuses on mining behavioral patterns from diverse digital data sources including social media interactions, web browsing histories, mobile app usage, and IoT sensor data. Students work with real-world datasets to extract meaningful behavioral insights using advanced pattern mining algorithms, sequence analysis, and anomaly detection techniques. The laboratory environment emphasizes practical implementation of mining workflows, from data preprocessing and feature extraction to pattern validation and interpretation. Students will master specialized tools for temporal pattern mining, association rule mining for behavioral sequences, and clustering techniques for user segmentation. Each lab session involves coding exercises using Python libraries such as mlxtend, scikit-learn, and specialized mining frameworks. Projects include mining customer journey patterns from e-commerce data, detecting unusual behavior in network traffic, and extracting routine patterns from location data. The course bridges theoretical mining concepts with practical applications in user behavior analysis, making it essential for students interested in user experience research, cybersecurity, marketing analytics, and human-computer interaction fields.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Pattern Mining Mastery**: Master advanced pattern mining algorithms for extracting behavioral sequences and anomalies from temporal digital data
2. **Laboratory Workflow Application**: Apply laboratory-based mining workflows to analyze real-world behavioral datasets using industry-standard tools and frameworks
3. **Insight Generation**: Develop expertise in validating and interpreting mined patterns to generate actionable insights about human digital behavior

## Required Materials

### Week 3: Advanced EDA and Statistical Analysis

### Week 5: Behavioral Data Understanding
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization Fundamentals

**Lab Activities:**

**Assessment Due:** Exploratory Data Analysis Lab Report: Customer Purchase Behavior

### Week 6: Sequential Pattern Mining Foundations
Focus on temporal sequence analysis, sliding window techniques, and behavioral sequence extraction from time-series data.

### Week 7: Association Rule Mining for Behavior
Market basket analysis applied to digital behavior, Apriori and FP-Growth algorithms for behavioral pattern discovery.

### Week 8: Clustering for User Segmentation
K-means, hierarchical clustering, and DBSCAN for identifying behavioral user groups and segments.

Statistical outlier detection, isolation forests, and one-class SVM for identifying unusual behavioral patterns.

Graph-based pattern mining, social network analysis, and community detection in behavioral networks.

Frequent pattern mining, sequential pattern mining algorithms (GSP, PrefixSpan), and specialized behavioral mining techniques.

Statistical significance testing, cross-validation for patterns, and business interpretation of mining results.

**Lab Activities:**

# ALGORITHMIC DECISION THEORY: MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATIONS OF MACHINE LEARNING SYSTEMS

**Course Code:** DS 4XX  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Linear Algebra, Multivariable Calculus, Probability Theory, Introduction to Machine Learning  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course explores the mathematical underpinnings of algorithmic decision-making in machine learning systems, emphasizing theoretical frameworks that govern how algorithms learn, adapt, and make predictions. Students will delve into the mathematical foundations of learning theory, examining concepts such as PAC learning, Rademacher complexity, and VC dimension to understand generalization bounds and sample complexity. The curriculum bridges statistical learning theory with computational complexity, investigating the theoretical limits of what can be learned efficiently. Topics include convex optimization theory for machine learning, kernel methods from a theoretical perspective, and the mathematical analysis of neural network expressivity. Students will study the theoretical guarantees of popular algorithms, analyze convergence properties, and explore the trade-offs between bias, variance, and computational efficiency. The course emphasizes proof-based learning, requiring students to derive key results and understand the mathematical reasoning behind algorithm design choices. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, students will develop a deep understanding of why certain machine learning approaches work, when they fail, and how theoretical insights can guide practical algorithm selection and hyperparameter tuning in real-world applications.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master the mathematical foundations of statistical learning theory**, including PAC learning, generalization bounds, and sample complexity analysis
2. **Apply theoretical frameworks to analyze the convergence properties and performance guarantees** of machine learning algorithms  
3. **Develop expertise in evaluating the theoretical trade-offs** between model complexity, computational efficiency, and generalization performance in machine learning systems

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

**Textbooks:**
- Shalev-Shwartz, S., & Ben-David, S. (2014). *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*. Cambridge University Press.
- Mohri, M., Rostamizadeh, A., & Talwalkar, A. (2018). *Foundations of Machine Learning* (2nd ed.). MIT Press.

- Jupyter Notebook or equivalent
- Access to university computing resources

### **Week 7: Convex Optimization for Machine LearningTopics:** Convex functions, gradient descent theory, convergence analysis

**Readings:** Shalev-Shwartz Ch. 12-14

### **Week 8: Online Learning and Regret AnalysisTopics:** Online learning algorithms, regret bounds, multiplicative weights
**Activities:** Online algorithm analysis
**Readings:** Shalev-Shwartz Ch. 21-22
**Assessment:** Midterm Exam - Fundamentals of Data Science Concepts and Basic Analysis

### **Week 9: Kernel Methods TheoryTopics:** Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, representer theorem, kernel complexity

**Readings:** Shalev-Shwartz Ch. 15-16

**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM

---

## Course Description

This comprehensive survey course explores the evolving landscape of data mining techniques across diverse domains, from social media sentiment extraction to bioinformatics pattern discovery. Students will journey through both classical and cutting-edge mining methodologies, examining how different industries 'excavate' valuable insights from their data repositories. The course provides broad exposure to various mining paradigms including association rule mining, anomaly detection, stream mining, graph mining, and text mining, while investigating real-world applications in finance, healthcare, e-commerce, and cybersecurity. Rather than diving deep into any single technique, this survey approach allows students to develop a comprehensive understanding of the data mining ecosystem, comparing strengths and limitations of different approaches. Through hands-on projects using industry-standard tools like Weka, RapidMiner, and Python libraries, students will gain practical experience while building a foundation to specialize in specific mining areas in advanced coursework. The course emphasizes critical evaluation of mining results, ethical considerations in data excavation, and the strategic selection of appropriate mining techniques for given problem domains.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Evaluate and compare** diverse data mining algorithms across multiple application domains to select optimal approaches for specific business and research scenarios

• **Apply survey methodology principles** to systematically analyze the data mining landscape and identify emerging trends in mining technologies

• **Develop proficiency** in using multiple mining tools and platforms to extract, analyze, and interpret patterns from heterogeneous data sources

# Course Syllabus

## Algorithmic Foundations of Pattern Discovery in Large-Scale Data Repositories

**Course Code:** DS 3400  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Data Structures and Algorithms (CS 2400), Statistics (STAT 2100), Linear Algebra (MATH 2200)  
**Meeting Time:** Tuesday/Thursday 2:00-3:30 PM  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

---

## Course Description

This course explores the theoretical underpinnings of extracting meaningful patterns from massive, heterogeneous data collections. Students will delve into the mathematical foundations of association rule mining, sequential pattern discovery, and graph mining algorithms. The curriculum emphasizes computational complexity analysis, algorithmic efficiency, and theoretical guarantees of mining techniques across diverse data types including transactional databases, time-series collections, and network structures. Through rigorous mathematical proofs and algorithmic design principles, students will understand how mining algorithms scale with data volume and dimensionality. The course covers advanced topics such as privacy-preserving mining, distributed mining architectures, and the theoretical limits of pattern discovery. Students will analyze the convergence properties of iterative mining algorithms, study approximation guarantees for NP-hard mining problems, and explore the statistical significance of discovered patterns. This theoretical foundation prepares students to design novel mining algorithms and critically evaluate existing approaches in research and industrial contexts.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Master the mathematical foundations of frequent itemset mining, sequential pattern mining, and subgraph mining algorithms  
• Apply complexity-theoretic analysis to evaluate the computational tractability of pattern discovery problems  
• Develop theoretical frameworks for assessing pattern significance and mining algorithm convergence properties  

## Required Materials

- **Textbook:** "Mining of Massive Datasets" by Leskovec, Rajaraman, and Ullman (3rd Edition)

### Week 5-6: Mathematical Foundations of Frequent Pattern Mining

**Class Meeting:** [days/times/location]

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This advanced course explores the intersection of behavioral psychology and data science to decode customer decision-making patterns and predict future behaviors. Students will dive deep into customer journey analytics, utilizing advanced statistical modeling techniques including survival analysis, propensity scoring, and sequential pattern mining to understand how customers interact with products and services over time. The course emphasizes real-world applications in e-commerce, digital marketing, and customer retention strategies. Students will work with large-scale transactional datasets, clickstream data, and multi-channel customer touchpoints to build sophisticated predictive models. Key topics include cohort analysis, customer lifetime value optimization, churn prediction models, recommendation system analytics, and A/B testing frameworks. ---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master advanced analytical techniques** for modeling customer behavior patterns including survival analysis, sequential pattern mining, and propensity scoring methodologies
2. **Apply machine learning algorithms** specifically designed for behavioral data to build predictive models for customer lifetime value, churn prediction, and personalization systems
3. **Develop expertise in translating** complex behavioral analytics findings into strategic business recommendations and data-driven customer intelligence solutions

---

# Probabilistic Reasoning and Statistical Inference in High-Dimensional Data
**Course Code:** DS 485 | **Credits:** 4 | **Semester:** Spring 2024

### Prerequisites
- Statistics (STAT 350) or equivalent
- Linear Algebra (MATH 250)  
- Programming experience in R or Python
- Calculus II (MATH 152)

## Course Description

This intensive course explores the statistical foundations underlying modern data science through the lens of high-dimensional data analysis. Students will master advanced probabilistic reasoning, Bayesian inference, and multivariate statistical methods essential for extracting meaningful insights from complex, large-scale datasets. The course emphasizes rigorous mathematical treatment of statistical concepts while maintaining practical relevance through hands-on implementation of algorithms from scratch. Topics include dimensionality reduction techniques, regularization methods, bootstrap and permutation testing, hierarchical modeling, and causal inference. Students will engage in weekly computational labs using R and Python, implementing statistical methods without relying on black-box functions. The intensive format includes daily problem-solving sessions, peer code reviews, and a capstone project involving real-world high-dimensional data analysis.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Advanced Statistical Mastery:** Develop expertise in statistical inference techniques for high-dimensional data including regularization, shrinkage estimators, and multiple testing corrections
2. **Algorithm Implementation:** Implement core statistical algorithms from mathematical foundations, demonstrating deep understanding of underlying probabilistic assumptions and computational complexity
3. **Bayesian Application:** Apply Bayesian reasoning and hierarchical modeling to real-world datasets, properly quantifying uncertainty and communicating statistical findings to technical and non-technical audiences

## Required Materials

- **Textbook:** "The Elements of Statistical Learning" by Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman (2nd Edition)
- **Software:** R (>= 4.0), RStudio, Python 3.8+, Jupyter Notebooks
- **Computing:** Laptop capable of running statistical software
- **Supplementary:** Selected journal articles and online resources (provided via LMS)

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of High-Dimensional Data Analysis
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization  
**Topics:**
- Univariate and bivariate analysis in high-dimensional contexts
- Statistical summaries and distribution analysis
- Visualization challenges with high-dimensional data
- Understanding correlation vs. causation in complex datasets

**Activity:** Interpreting Correlation vs Causation in Customer Churn Analysis (65 min)  
**Readings:** Course packet Ch. 1; Hastie et al. Ch. 1

### Week 2: Feature Engineering Foundations
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning  
**Topics:**
- Feature transformation and scaling techniques
- Categorical encoding strategies for high-dimensional data
- Mathematical transformations and their statistical properties
- Domain knowledge integration in feature creation

**Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data (55 min)  
**Readings:** Hastie et al. Ch. 3; Selected papers on feature engineering

### Week 3: Probabilistic Foundations for High-Dimensional Inference
**Topics:**
- Multivariate probability distributions
- Curse of dimensionality and its statistical implications
- Maximum likelihood estimation in high dimensions
- Asymptotic behavior of estimators

**Activity:** Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis (75 min)  
**Due:** Problem Set 1

### Week 4: Regularization and Shrinkage Methods
**Topics:**
- Ridge regression: theory and implementation
- LASSO: sparse solutions and variable selection
- Elastic net and generalizations
- Cross-validation for regularization parameter selection

**Activity:** Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Learning Curves Analysis (85 min)  
**Readings:** Hastie et al. Ch. 3.4, 18.4

### Week 5: Bayesian Inference Fundamentals
**Topics:**
- Bayesian vs. frequentist paradigms
- Prior specification and sensitivity analysis
- Conjugate priors and posterior computation
- Bayesian model comparison

**Activity:** Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Selection for Imbalanced Healthcare Dataset (140 min)  
**Due:** Problem Set 2

### Week 6: Hierarchical and Multilevel Modeling
**Topics:**
- Random effects and mixed models
- Bayesian hierarchical models
- Partial pooling and shrinkage
- Applications in genomics and social science

**Assessment:Quiz 1:** Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Assessment (100 points)

### Week 7: Dimensionality Reduction Theory
**Topics:**
- Principal Component Analysis: mathematical foundations
- Singular Value Decomposition theory
- Random projections and Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma
- Manifold learning principles

**Activity:** Interpreting Customer Segmentation Results from K-Means Clustering Analysis (60 min)  
**Readings:** Hastie et al. Ch. 14.5

### Week 8: Advanced Dimensionality Reduction
**Topics:**
- Independent Component Analysis
- t-SNE and UMAP theory
- Sparse PCA and dictionary learning
- Nonlinear dimensionality reduction

**Due:** Problem Set 3

### Week 9: Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate
**Topics:**
- Family-wise error rate control
- Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
- q-values and local false discovery rates
- Applications in genomics

**Activity:** Analyzing Bias Propagation in Multi-Stage Machine Learning Pipelines (110 min)

### Week 10: Bootstrap and Resampling Methods
**Topics:**
- Bootstrap theory and consistency
- Parametric vs. nonparametric bootstrap
- Permutation tests and exact inference
- Subsampling methods

**Assessment:Presentation:** Data Science Process Presentation: From Question to Insight (100 points)

### Week 11: Causal Inference in Observational Data
**Topics:**
- Potential outcomes framework
- Propensity score methods
- Instrumental variables
- Difference-in-differences

**Due:** Problem Set 4

### Week 12: High-Dimensional Hypothesis Testing
**Topics:**
- Sparse signal detection
- Minimax testing theory
- Higher criticism and innovations
- Applications to genomics data

**Activity:** Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Healthcare Risk Assessment (220 min)

### Week 13: Model Selection and Information Criteria
**Topics:**
- AIC, BIC, and extensions to high dimensions
- Cross-validation theory
- Information-theoretic model selection
- Prediction vs. explanation trade-offs

**Assessment:Discussion:** Bias Detection and Mitigation in Machine Learning Systems (100 points)

### Week 14: Advanced Topics and Applications
**Topics:**
- Sparse graphical models
- High-dimensional time series
- Functional data analysis
- Recent developments in statistical learning

**Activity:** Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Sales Analysis (55 min)

### Week 15: Capstone Project Presentations
**Topics:**
- Student project presentations
- Peer review and feedback
- Integration of course concepts
- Future directions in statistical inference

**Assessment:Portfolio:** End-to-End Machine Learning Portfolio (100 points)  
**Assessment:Project:** Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Project (100 points)

# Visual Storytelling with Data: From Pixels to Persuasion

**Course Code:** DS 3XX  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Introduction to Statistics, Programming Fundamentals  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

## Course Description

This survey course explores how data visualization serves as a bridge between raw data and human understanding across diverse domains. Students examine visualization techniques from traditional statistical graphics to cutting-edge interactive dashboards, virtual reality data environments, and artistic data representations. The course surveys real-world applications spanning journalism, business intelligence, scientific research, public policy, and social media analytics. Through hands-on projects, students learn to critically evaluate visualization choices, understand cognitive principles behind effective visual communication, and master tools ranging from Python/R libraries to specialized platforms like Tableau, D3.js, and emerging VR/AR visualization frameworks. Emphasis is placed on ethical considerations in data presentation, accessibility in visual design, and the psychological impact of visual choices on decision-making.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Evaluate and critique** visualization techniques across multiple domains including journalism, business, science, and public policy
2. **Apply cognitive and perceptual principles** to design effective visual narratives that communicate complex data insights to diverse audiences
3. **Develop proficiency** in a survey of visualization tools and platforms, from programming libraries to enterprise dashboards and emerging technologies

## Required Materials

- **Textbook:** *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* by Edward Tufte
- **Software:** Python (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, plotly), Tableau Desktop (student license), access to D3.js
- **Hardware:** Laptop capable of running visualization software
- **Platform:** Course materials available on Canvas LMS

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Visual Data Communication
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization Fundamentals
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Univariate Analysis: examining individual variables through measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape using histograms, box plots, and summary statistics
  - Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis: exploring relationships between variables using correlation analysis, scatter plots, cross-tabulations, and heatmaps
- **Activities:** Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Customer Purchase Behavior (50 min)
- **Readings:** Tufte Ch. 1-2

### Week 2: Data Quality and Visual Integrity
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Univariate Analysis: Statistical examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape
  - Data Quality Assessment: Systematic identification and handling of missing values, outliers, duplicates, and inconsistencies in datasets
- **Activities:** Interpreting Statistical Bias in Real-World Survey Data (75 min)
- **Assessment:** Data Science Fundamentals Quiz (Due Friday)

### Week 3: Python for Visual Storytelling
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Python
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Univariate Analysis: Statistical and visual examination of individual variables including distribution shapes, central tendency, and variability
  - Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis: Exploration of relationships between two or more variables using correlation coefficients, scatter plots, and cross-tabulations
- **Activities:** Interpreting Customer Churn Patterns Through Exploratory Data Analysis (85 min)

### Week 4: Advanced Python Visualization
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Python: Uncovering Insights Through Visualization and Statistical Analysis
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Data Profiling: Systematic examination of data structure, completeness, and quality metrics
  - Univariate Analysis: Statistical analysis of individual variables including distribution shape, central tendency, and variability measures
- **Activities:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps for Customer Churn Prediction (60 min)

### Week 5: Understanding Relationships in Data
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature transformation: Mathematical operations applied to variables to improve their relationship with target variables
  - Feature selection: Statistical and algorithmic methods to identify the most predictive subset of features
- **Activities:** Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Dataset Analysis (60 min)

### Week 6: Advanced Feature Visualization
**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning: Creating Predictive Variables from Raw Data
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature scaling and normalization: techniques like StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler
  - Categorical encoding methods: one-hot encoding, target encoding, and hash encoding strategies
- **Activities:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data (55 min)

### Week 7: Predictive Modeling Visualization
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Predictive Modeling
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature Creation: generating new variables from existing data through mathematical operations, binning, encoding
  - Feature Selection: systematic methods to identify and retain the most predictive variables
- **Activities:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Matrices in Customer Churn Analysis (80 min)

### Week 8: Midterm Week
- **Assessment:** Customer Segmentation Analysis and Predictive Modeling Exam

### Week 9: Advanced Correlation Analysis
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Predictive Modeling
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature Engineering: The process of creating new variables from existing data to improve model performance
  - Feature Selection: Statistical and algorithmic methods to identify and retain the most informative variables
- **Activities:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Matrices for Customer Churn Prediction (50 min)

### Week 10: Machine Learning Visualization Techniques
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature transformation: Mathematical operations to modify existing features including normalization, standardization
  - Categorical encoding: Techniques for converting categorical variables into numerical representations
- **Activities:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis (60 min)

### Week 11: Causation vs. Correlation in Visual Narratives
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature Engineering: The process of creating new features from existing data through mathematical transformations
  - Curse of Dimensionality: The phenomenon where model performance degrades as the number of features increases
- **Activities:** Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Churn Analysis (60 min)
- **Assessment:** Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Lab Report (Due Friday)

### Week 12: Ethical Considerations in Data Visualization
- **Focus:** Bias in visual representation, accessibility, and responsible data storytelling
- **Assessment:** Ethical AI and Bias Mitigation Discussion Forum Opens

### Week 13: Interactive and Emerging Technologies
- **Topics:** Dashboard design, VR/AR visualization, real-time data visualization

# Course Syllabus

## CS 3820: Algorithmic Intelligence: From Raw Data to Predictive Systems

**Semester:** Fall 2024  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** CS 2110 (Data Structures), STAT 2020 (Statistics), MATH 2310 (Calculus I)  
- Lecture: MWF 10:00-10:50 AM
- Lab: T/Th 2:00-4:00 PM (mandatory)

---

## Course Description

This intensive course transforms students into machine learning practitioners through hands-on development of complete predictive systems. Students work with real-world messy datasets to build end-to-end ML pipelines, from data ingestion and preprocessing to model deployment and monitoring. The course emphasizes algorithmic thinking and practical implementation over theoretical foundations, requiring students to code solutions from scratch before using high-level libraries. Through weekly hackathons and industry case studies, students tackle complex problems in computer vision, natural language processing, and time series forecasting. The curriculum integrates modern MLOps practices, including version control for models, automated testing, and continuous integration. Students collaborate on a semester-long capstone project with external industry partners, delivering production-ready ML systems. The intensive format includes mandatory lab sessions, peer code reviews, and real-time debugging workshops. By course completion, students possess a portfolio of deployed ML applications and the technical confidence to architect scalable predictive systems in professional environments.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design and implement complete machine learning pipelines** from raw data collection through model deployment and monitoring  
• **Master algorithmic problem-solving** by coding ML algorithms from fundamentals before utilizing advanced frameworks  
• **Develop production-ready predictive systems** using industry-standard MLOps practices and collaborative development workflows  
• **Apply machine learning techniques** across diverse domains including computer vision, NLP, and time series analysis through intensive project-based learning

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Data Analysis
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Statistical Visualization
- **Concepts:**
  - Descriptive Statistics: Measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape including mean, median, mode, variance, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis
  - Data Distribution Analysis: Understanding normal, skewed, and multimodal distributions through histograms, box plots, Q-Q plots, and statistical tests for normality
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Real-World Sales Analytics (60 min)
- **Assignment:** Data profiling report on provided messy dataset

### Week 2: Data Understanding and Visualization
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization Fundamentals
- **Concepts:**
  - Data profiling: Systematic examination of dataset structure, completeness, and quality including missing value patterns and data type validation
  - Distribution analysis: Understanding data spread, central tendency, skewness, and kurtosis through histograms, box plots, and statistical measures
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Using Real-World Sales Dataset (90 min)
- **Mini-Hackathon:** Visualization dashboard creation

### Week 3: Relationship Analysis
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization with Python
- **Concepts:**
  - Univariate Analysis - Statistical examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape
  - Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis - Exploration of relationships between multiple variables using correlation matrices, scatter plots, and cross-tabulations
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data (65 min)
- **Quiz:** Customer Churn Analysis and Model Development Quiz (100 points)

### Week 4: Advanced Correlation Analysis
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Feature Engineering
- **Concepts:**
  - Univariate Analysis - Statistical summaries, distribution shapes, and central tendency measures for individual variables
  - Bivariate Analysis - Correlation analysis, scatter plots, and relationship identification between variable pairs
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Estate Data Analysis (85 min)

### Week 5: Feature Engineering Fundamentals
**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning
- **Concepts:**
  - Categorical Encoding - Methods for converting categorical variables into numerical representations suitable for machine learning algorithms
  - Feature Scaling - Techniques like standardization and normalization to ensure features contribute equally to model training
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Behavior Data (55 min)
- **Discussion:** Data Science Methodology Discussion: Comparing CRISP-DM and KDD Approaches (100 points)

### Week 6: Advanced Feature Engineering
**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning
- **Concepts:**
  - One-hot encoding and target encoding - Methods for converting categorical variables into numerical representations suitable for machine learning algorithms
  - Feature scaling and normalization - Techniques including StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler to ensure features contribute equally to model training
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Statistical Relationships in Customer Churn Analysis (85 min)
- **Mini-Hackathon:** Feature engineering competition

### Week 7: Feature Selection and Engineering
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts:**
  - Feature scaling and normalization - techniques like StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler to ensure features are on comparable scales
  - Categorical encoding methods - one-hot encoding, target encoding, and ordinal encoding strategies for converting categorical variables to numerical format
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models: A Comparative Analysis Activity (60 min)

### Week 8: Advanced Feature Selection
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts:**
  - Feature Engineering - The process of creating new features from existing data through mathematical transformations, domain knowledge application, and data combination techniques
  - Feature Selection - Statistical and algorithmic methods for identifying the most relevant subset of features, including filter, wrapper, and embedded methods
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models for Customer Churn Prediction (75 min)
- **Lab Report:** Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Development and Model Interpretability Analysis (100 points)

### Week 9: Model Implementation from Scratch
- **Focus:** Coding fundamental ML algorithms without libraries
- **Topics:** Linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees from scratch
- **Mini-Hackathon:** Algorithm implementation challenge

### Week 10: Model Evaluation and Interpretation
- **Focus:** Understanding model performance and interpretability
- **Topics:** Cross-validation, bias-variance tradeoff, model diagnostics
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Confusion Matrix Results for Multi-Class Classification Problems (70 min)

### Week 11: Computer Vision Applications
- **Focus:** Image processing and computer vision ML pipelines
- **Topics:** CNN architectures, image preprocessing, transfer learning
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Customer Churn Analysis Results from Different Machine Learning Models (70 min)
- **Mini-Hackathon:** Image classification challenge

### Week 12: Natural Language Processing
- **Focus:** Text processing and NLP applications
- **Topics:** Text preprocessing, word embeddings, sentiment analysis
- **Project Milestone:** Capstone project mid-term presentation

### Week 13: Time Series Forecasting
- **Focus:** Temporal data analysis and prediction
- **Topics:** Time series decomposition, ARIMA, seasonal patterns
- **Mini-Hackathon:** Forecasting competition

### Week 14: MLOps and Deployment
- **Focus:** Production deployment and monitoring
- **Topics:** Model versioning, CI/CD for ML, monitoring systems
- **Capstone Work:** Final system integration

### Week 15: Final Presentations and Portfolio Review
- **Capstone Presentations:** End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline: Business Case Presentation (100 points)
- **Portfolio Review:** Student project demonstrations
- **Industry Partner Feedback:** External evaluation sessions

# Data-Driven Decision Making for Business Performance
**Course Syllabus - Spring 2024**

## Course Description

This course bridges the gap between raw data and strategic business decisions by teaching students how to transform organizational data into actionable intelligence. Students learn to identify key performance indicators, design executive dashboards, and communicate data insights to stakeholders across different business functions. The curriculum emphasizes practical applications in sales forecasting, customer segmentation, market analysis, and operational efficiency measurement. Through hands-on projects using real business datasets, students master essential tools like Excel, Tableau, and SQL while developing critical thinking skills to evaluate data quality and bias. The course covers fundamental statistical concepts within business contexts, teaching students to recognize patterns, trends, and anomalies that impact organizational performance. Students work on collaborative projects that simulate real-world business scenarios, learning to present findings to non-technical audiences and make recommendations based on data analysis. By course completion, students understand how to leverage data science techniques to solve common business challenges, create compelling visualizations, and establish data governance practices. This practical approach prepares students for entry-level business analyst roles or advanced coursework in data science, emphasizing the strategic value of data in modern organizations.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design and implement business intelligence dashboards** that translate complex data into actionable insights for organizational decision-making
• **Apply statistical analysis techniques** to solve real-world business problems including sales forecasting, customer behavior analysis, and operational optimization
• **Develop proficiency in communicating data-driven recommendations** to diverse stakeholders through compelling visualizations and executive presentations

## Required Materials

### Textbooks
- **Primary:** "Practical Statistics for Data Scientists" by Peter Bruce & Andrew Bruce (2nd Edition)
- **Supplementary:** "Storytelling with Data" by Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic

### Software & Tools
- Microsoft Excel (Office 365)
- Tableau Desktop (Student License)
- SQL Server Management Studio
- Python 3.x with Jupyter Notebooks
- Access to university's business database systems

### Hardware Requirements
- Laptop capable of running data analysis software
- Minimum 8GB RAM recommended

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Course Introduction & Data Landscape
**Topics:** Course overview, role of data in business decisions, data types and sources
**Readings:** Chapter 1-2 from primary textbook
**Activities:** Course introduction and business data exploration

### Week 2: Exploratory Data Analysis Fundamentals
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Statistical Visualization

- Univariate Analysis - Statistical examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape
- Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis - Exploring relationships between two or more variables using correlation analysis, cross-tabulations, and multi-dimensional visualizations
**Activities:** Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Purchase Data Analysis (60 minutes)

### Week 3: Data Quality and Assessment
