# THERMAL ENGINES AND ENERGY TRANSFORMATIONS: FROM STEAM POWER TO QUANTUM HEAT MACHINES

**Course Code:** PHYS 3420  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** PHYS 2210 (Modern Physics), PHYS 2220 (Thermodynamics), MATH 2250 (Differential Equations)  

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This comprehensive course explores the fundamental principles of thermodynamics through the lens of practical energy conversion systems and emerging quantum thermal technologies. Students will investigate classical heat engines, refrigeration cycles, and power generation systems while developing a deep understanding of entropy, statistical mechanics, and the laws of thermodynamics. The curriculum bridges historical developments in steam engines and internal combustion systems with cutting-edge research in thermoelectric devices, heat pumps, and quantum thermal machines. Laboratory components include hands-on construction and analysis of Stirling engines, calorimetry experiments, and computational modeling of thermal systems. Students will examine real-world applications including automotive engines, power plant cycles, renewable energy systems, and microscale thermal devices. The course emphasizes both theoretical rigor and practical problem-solving, preparing students to analyze complex thermal systems and evaluate energy efficiency in various technological contexts. Advanced topics include irreversible thermodynamics, thermal fluctuations, and the thermodynamics of information processing, providing a foundation for graduate study or careers in energy engineering, materials science, and emerging quantum technologies.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master the fundamental laws of thermodynamics** and apply them to analyze complex thermal cycles and energy conversion systems
• **Develop comprehensive skills in statistical mechanics** to understand the microscopic origins of thermal phenomena and entropy
• **Gain practical expertise in designing, modeling, and optimizing thermal engines** while evaluating their environmental and economic impacts

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

**Textbook:** Callen, H.B. *Thermodynamics and an Introduction to Thermostatistics*, 2nd Edition, Wiley  
**Supplementary Texts:** 
- Kittel, C. & Kroemer, H. *Thermal Physics*, 2nd Edition, W.H. Freeman
- Bejan, A. *Advanced Engineering Thermodynamics*, 4th Edition, Wiley

**Lab Manual:** Available on course website  
**Software:** Python with NumPy/SciPy (free), MATLAB (campus license available)  
**Calculator:** Scientific calculator required for exams

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Historical Foundations and First Law
**Topics:** Course introduction, historical development of steam engines, energy conservation principles, First Law applications  
**Readings:** Callen Ch. 1-2  

### Week 2: Second Law and Entropy Introduction
**Topics:** Carnot cycles, entropy concept, irreversibility, Clausius inequality  
**Readings:** Callen Ch. 3-4  

### Week 3: Statistical Foundations of Thermodynamics
**Topics:** Microscopic vs. macroscopic perspectives, Boltzmann distribution, partition functions  
**Readings:** Kittel & Kroemer Ch. 1-3  

### Week 4: Heat Engines and Efficiency Analysis
**Topics:** Otto, Diesel, and Brayton cycles, efficiency calculations, real engine performance  
**Readings:** Callen Ch. 5  

### Week 5: Refrigeration Cycles and Heat Pumps
**Topics:** Vapor compression cycles, COP analysis, environmental considerations  
**Readings:** Supplementary materials  

### Week 6: Phase Transitions and Steam Power
**Topics:** Phase diagrams, steam tables, Rankine cycle analysis, power plant operations  
**Readings:** Callen Ch. 9  

### Week 7: Advanced Statistical Mechanics
**Topics:** Maxwell-Boltzmann, Fermi-Dirac, and Bose-Einstein statistics  
**Readings:** Kittel & Kroemer Ch. 4-6  

### Week 8: **MIDTERM EXAMINATION**

### Week 9: Thermoelectric Devices
**Topics:** Seebeck effect, Peltier effect, thermoelectric generators and coolers, figure of merit  
**Readings:** Supplementary materials  

### Week 10: Irreversible Thermodynamics
**Topics:** Linear response theory, Onsager relations, entropy production  
**Readings:** Advanced supplementary materials  

### Week 11: Thermal Fluctuations and Noise
**Topics:** Johnson noise, thermal fluctuation-dissipation theorem, Brownian motion  
**Readings:** Advanced supplementary materials  

### Week 12: Quantum Thermal Machines
**Topics:** Quantum heat engines, quantum refrigerators, coherence effects  
**Readings:** Recent research papers (provided)  

### Week 13: Energy Storage and Conversion Systems
**Topics:** Fuel cells, batteries, compressed air storage, thermal energy storage  
**Readings:** Bejan Ch. 10-12  

### Week 14: Renewable Energy Thermodynamics
**Topics:** Solar thermal, geothermal, biomass conversion, thermodynamic limits  
**Readings:** Supplementary materials  

### Week 15: Information Thermodynamics and Future Directions
**Topics:** Maxwell's demon, Landauer's principle, computation and thermodynamics  
**Readings:** Recent research papers (provided)  

### Week 16: **FINAL EXAMINATION WEEK**

# The Quantum Zoo: Building Blocks of Matter and Their Interactions

**Course Code:** PHYS 3350  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** PHYS 2420 (Modern Physics), MATH 2450 (Differential Equations)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM, Lab: W 2:00-5:00 PM  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

---

## Course Description

This foundational course explores the fundamental particles that constitute all matter and the forces governing their interactions. Students will journey through the Standard Model of particle physics, beginning with the historical discovery of subatomic particles and progressing to modern understanding of quarks, leptons, and gauge bosons. The course emphasizes conceptual understanding through mathematical formalism, covering particle classification, conservation laws, symmetries, and interaction mechanisms. Laboratory components include cosmic ray detection, bubble chamber analysis, and computer simulations of particle collisions. Students will analyze real experimental data from major particle accelerators, learning to identify particle signatures and decay patterns. Topics include the electromagnetic, weak, and strong nuclear forces, particle-antiparticle relationships, and the Higgs mechanism. The course bridges classical physics concepts with quantum field theory foundations, preparing students for advanced study in high-energy physics. Special attention is given to experimental techniques, detector principles, and the role of particle accelerators in modern research.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master** the classification and properties of fundamental particles within the Standard Model framework  
• **Apply** conservation laws and symmetry principles to analyze particle interactions and decay processes  
• **Develop** practical expertise in interpreting experimental particle physics data and detector signatures  

## Required Materials

- **Textbook:** "Introduction to Elementary Particles" by David Griffiths (2nd Edition)
- **Supplementary:** Selected readings from "Particle Physics: A Very Short Introduction" by Frank Close
- **Software:** ROOT data analysis framework (free download)
- **Lab Manual:** Available on course website
- **Calculator:** Scientific calculator required

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Particle Physics
**Module:** Wave-Particle Duality and the Photoelectric Effect  
**Topics:**
- Photoelectric Effect - emission of electrons from a material when light strikes its surface, demonstrating particle nature of light
- Work Function - minimum energy required to remove an electron from a material's surface, measured in electron volts (eV)
- Historical context and early particle discoveries

**Activity:** *Analyzing Energy Transformations in a Compound Pendulum System with Damping* (90 minutes)

### Week 2: Electromagnetic Foundations I
**Module:** Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law  
**Topics:**
- Magnetic Flux (Φ): The measure of magnetic field lines passing through a surface, calculated as Φ = B⃗ · A⃗ = BA cos θ
- Faraday's Law: The induced EMF equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt
- Applications to particle accelerators and detectors

### Week 3: Wave Properties and Quantum Mechanics
**Module:** Simple Harmonic Motion: Springs, Pendulums, and Oscillations  
**Topics:**
- Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) - periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium (F = -kx)
- Period (T) and Frequency (f) - time for one complete oscillation and number of oscillations per unit time, related by f = 1/T
- Quantum harmonic oscillator as particle physics foundation

**Activity:** *Analyzing Energy Transformation Inefficiencies in Multi-Stage Mechanical Systems* (90 minutes)

### Week 4: Wave Interference and Detection Principles
**Module:** Wave Interference and Standing Waves  
**Topics:**
- Principle of Superposition - waves combine algebraically when occupying the same space, with amplitudes adding vectorially
- Constructive Interference - waves combine to produce maximum amplitude when phase difference is 0, 2π, 4π, etc.
- Particle wave functions and detection principles

**Activity:** *Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Slit Diffraction Systems* (125 minutes)

### Week 5: Advanced Wave Phenomena
**Module:** Wave Interference and Diffraction Phenomena  
**Topics:**
- Constructive interference - waves combining in phase to produce maximum amplitude when path difference equals integer multiples of wavelength
- Destructive interference - waves combining out of phase to produce minimum amplitude when path difference equals odd multiples of half-wavelength
- Matter waves and particle detection

**Assessment:** *Advanced Quantum Mechanics and Electrodynamics Comprehensive Quiz* (100 points)

### Week 6: Oscillatory Motion and Field Theory
**Module:** Simple Harmonic Motion and Oscillations  
**Topics:**
- Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) - periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium position
- Angular frequency (ω) - measure of how rapidly oscillation occurs, related to period by ω = 2π/T
- Field oscillations and virtual particles

**Activity:** *Analyzing Multi-Component Electrical Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting* (75 minutes)

### Week 7: The Standard Model Framework
**Topics:**
- Fundamental particles: quarks, leptons, gauge bosons
- The four fundamental forces
- Symmetries and conservation laws
- Particle classification schemes

**Activity:** *Analyzing Electromagnetic Interference in Circuit Design: Multi-Variable Impact Assessment* (120 minutes)

### Week 8: Quarks and the Strong Force
**Topics:**
- Quark model and flavor quantum numbers
- Color charge and quantum chromodynamics (QCD)
- Confinement and asymptotic freedom
- Hadron spectroscopy

### Week 9: Leptons and the Weak Force
**Topics:**
- Electron, muon, and tau families
- Neutrino properties and detection
- Weak nuclear force and W/Z bosons
- Parity violation and CP violation

**Activity:** *Analyzing Electromagnetic Interference in Multi-Frequency Circuit Systems* (120 minutes)

**Assessment:** *Electromagnetic Induction Laboratory Investigation and Design Project* (100 points) - Due

### Week 10: Electromagnetic Interactions
**Topics:**
- Quantum electrodynamics (QED)
- Photon exchange and virtual particles
- Feynman diagrams introduction
- Cross-sections and decay rates

**Activity:** *Electromagnetic Induction Circuit Analysis: Comparing Faraday's Law Applications in Real-World Systems* (100 minutes)

### Week 11: Particle Interactions and Decay
**Topics:**
- Conservation laws in particle physics
- Selection rules and forbidden decays
- Resonances and particle lifetimes
- Experimental signatures

**Assessment:** *Electromagnetic Induction Laboratory Analysis Report* (100 points) - Due

### Week 12: Symmetries and Conservation Laws
**Topics:**
- Noether's theorem
- Isospin and strangeness
- Time reversal and CPT theorem
- Spontaneous symmetry breaking

**Activity:** *Analyzing Multi-Loop Circuit Breakdown: Kirchhoff's Laws Application* (130 minutes)

### Week 13: The Higgs Mechanism
**Topics:**
- Spontaneous symmetry breaking
- Higgs field and Higgs boson
- Mass generation mechanism
- LHC discovery and implications

**Activity:** *Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems Using Phase Space Diagrams* (165 minutes)

**Assessment:** *Quantum Entanglement and Bell's Theorem: Implications for Local Realism* Discussion (100 points)

### Week 14: Experimental Techniques
**Topics:**
- Particle accelerators and colliders
- Detector principles and technologies
- Data acquisition and trigger systems
- Statistical analysis methods

**Activity:** *Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems: The Three-Body Problem in Astrophysical Contexts* (120 minutes)

### Week 15: Frontiers and Applications
**Topics:**
- Beyond the Standard Model
- Dark matter and supersymmetry
- Particle physics applications in technology
- Current research frontiers

**Assessment:** *Advanced Physics Research Portfolio: Quantum Mechanics Applications* (100 points) - Due

### Week 16: Final Exam Week
**Final Exam:** Comprehensive exam covering all course material

course_info.title: Electromagnetic Wave Propagation in Complex Media
course_info.description: This specialized course examines the behavior of electromagnetic waves as they propagate through inhomogeneous, anisotropic, and nonlinear media. Students will explore advanced topics including metamaterials, photonic crystals, plasma physics, and biological tissues from an electromagnetic perspective. The course emphasizes mathematical modeling using Maxwell's equations in complex geometries, numerical simulation techniques, and experimental characterization methods. Key applications include optical fiber communications, radar systems, medical imaging technologies, and emerging metamaterial devices. Laboratory components involve hands-on experience with vector network analyzers, spectrum analyzers, and electromagnetic simulation software. Students will investigate phenomena such as surface plasmons, negative refractive index materials, electromagnetic bandgaps, and nonlinear optical effects. The curriculum bridges fundamental electromagnetic theory with cutting-edge research in photonics and RF engineering. Projects include designing frequency-selective surfaces, analyzing wave scattering from random media, and modeling electromagnetic compatibility in electronic systems. This course prepares students for graduate research or careers in telecommunications, defense technology, medical devices, and emerging fields like quantum photonics.
learning_objectives: Students will master advanced electromagnetic wave theory including propagation in anisotropic, dispersive, and nonlinear media
Students will apply numerical modeling techniques to solve complex electromagnetic boundary value problems in realistic geometries
Students will develop practical expertise in electromagnetic characterization methods and interpretation of experimental data from complex media

course_info.title: Quantum Photonics and Nonlinear Optical Phenomena
course_info.description: This intensive upper-level course explores the quantum nature of light and advanced nonlinear optical processes that govern modern photonic technologies. Students will investigate quantum states of light, including squeezed states, entangled photons, and coherent states, while mastering the mathematical frameworks of second-order and third-order nonlinear optics. The course emphasizes hands-on laboratory work with femtosecond lasers, nonlinear crystals, and single-photon detection systems. Weekly problem sets involve complex calculations of parametric amplification, four-wave mixing, and quantum interference effects. Students will design and simulate photonic devices including quantum key distribution systems, optical frequency combs, and metamaterial structures. The intensive format includes three lectures and two extended laboratory sessions per week, culminating in an independent research project on cutting-edge topics such as topological photonics, plasmonics, or quantum sensing. This course bridges fundamental quantum mechanics with practical applications in quantum computing, telecommunications, and precision metrology, preparing students for graduate research or careers in the rapidly expanding photonics industry.
learning_objectives: Students will master quantum optical theory including field quantization, photon statistics, and non-classical states of light
Students will apply nonlinear optical principles to analyze frequency conversion, optical switching, and parametric processes in various media
Students will develop expertise in advanced experimental techniques including ultrafast spectroscopy, single-photon detection, and nanophotonic device characterization
course_info.prerequisites: Modern Physics, Electromagnetic Theory, Mathematical Methods in Physics (differential equations, Fourier analysis), and either Quantum Mechanics I or Advanced Optics Laboratory
course_info.target_audience: Junior and senior physics majors, electrical engineering students with strong physics background, and pre-graduate students interested in quantum optics, photonics research, or optical engineering careers

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This intensive upper-level course explores the quantum nature of light and advanced nonlinear optical processes that govern modern photonic technologies. Students will investigate quantum states of light, including squeezed states, entangled photons, and coherent states, while mastering the mathematical frameworks of second-order and third-order nonlinear optics. The course emphasizes hands-on laboratory work with femtosecond lasers, nonlinear crystals, and single-photon detection systems. Weekly problem sets involve complex calculations of parametric amplification, four-wave mixing, and quantum interference effects. Students will design and simulate photonic devices including quantum key distribution systems, optical frequency combs, and metamaterial structures. The intensive format includes three lectures and two extended laboratory sessions per week, culminating in an independent research project on cutting-edge topics such as topological photonics, plasmonics, or quantum sensing. This course bridges fundamental quantum mechanics with practical applications in quantum computing, telecommunications, and precision metrology, preparing students for graduate research or careers in the rapidly expanding photonics industry.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will:

• Master quantum optical theory including field quantization, photon statistics, and non-classical states of light
• Apply nonlinear optical principles to analyze frequency conversion, optical switching, and parametric processes in various media  
• Develop expertise in advanced experimental techniques including ultrafast spectroscopy, single-photon detection, and nanophotonic device characterization

---

# Thermal Systems Engineering: From Heat Engines to Quantum Devices
**Physics 485 | Undergraduate Capstone Course**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer, Statistical Mechanics  
**Duration:** 15-week semester  
**Class Meeting:** TR 2:00-3:50 PM  

### Course Description
This capstone course bridges classical thermodynamics with cutting-edge thermal technologies, challenging students to design and analyze real-world thermal systems. Students will investigate the thermodynamic principles governing everything from automotive engines and power plants to thermoelectric devices and quantum heat engines. The course emphasizes hands-on problem-solving through industry-relevant projects, including optimization of heat pump systems, analysis of renewable energy thermal storage, and exploration of nanoscale heat transfer phenomena. Students will work in teams to tackle authentic engineering challenges, such as improving the efficiency of solar thermal collectors or designing thermal management systems for electronic devices. Advanced topics include irreversible thermodynamics, statistical mechanics applications to thermal systems, and the thermodynamics of phase transitions in novel materials. The capstone project requires students to propose, design, and theoretically validate an innovative thermal system solution to address contemporary energy challenges.

### Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
• Design and optimize complex thermal systems by integrating classical thermodynamics with modern heat transfer principles
• Analyze and solve multi-scale thermal problems ranging from macroscopic heat engines to quantum thermal devices using advanced computational and analytical methods
• Evaluate the thermodynamic performance of emerging energy technologies and propose innovative solutions to contemporary thermal engineering challenges

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Classical Thermodynamic Foundations and System Analysis
**Topics:** Review of thermodynamic laws, system boundaries, energy balance equations
**Activity:** Analyzing Energy Transformations in a Compound Pendulum System with Damping (90 min)

### Week 2: Heat Engine Cycles and Performance Optimization
**Topics:** Carnot, Otto, Diesel, and Brayton cycles; efficiency analysis
**Activity:** Analyzing Energy Transformation Inefficiencies in Multi-Stage Mechanical Systems (90 min)

### Week 3: Advanced Heat Transfer Mechanisms
**Topics:** Conduction, convection, and radiation in complex geometries
**Activity:** Multi-Variable Circuit Analysis: Decomposing Complex DC Networks Using Nodal and Mesh Methods (120 min)

### Week 4: Thermoelectric Phenomena and Quantum Effects
**Topics:** Seebeck, Peltier, and Thomson effects; quantum thermal transport
**Activity:** Analyzing Quantum Tunneling Probability Variations in Multi-Barrier Semiconductor Heterostructures (100 min)

### Week 5: Statistical Mechanics in Thermal Systems
**Topics:** Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, phonon transport, electron-phonon interactions
**Activity:** Electromagnetic Spectrum Anomaly Analysis: Investigating Stellar Classification Discrepancies (100 min)

### Week 6: Electromagnetic Coupling in Thermal Devices
**Topics:** Electromagnetic induction in thermal systems, magnetic cooling
**Module:** Magnetic Flux (Φ) - the measure of magnetic field lines passing through a surface, calculated as Φ = B⃗ · A⃗ = BA cos θ
**Module:** Faraday's Law - the induced EMF in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt

### Week 7: Wave-Based Heat Transfer and Thermal Radiation
**Topics:** Thermal radiation as electromagnetic waves, phonon wave interactions
**Module:** Principle of Superposition - waves combine algebraically when occupying the same space, with amplitudes adding vectorially
**Module:** Constructive Interference - waves combine to produce maximum amplitude when phase difference is 0, 2π, 4π, etc.
**Activity:** Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Slit Diffraction Systems (125 min)

### Week 8: Midterm Assessment Period
**Assessment:** Advanced Electromagnetic Induction Laboratory Investigation (Lab Report - 100 points)

### Week 9: Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena
**Topics:** Phase diagrams, critical points, latent heat in novel materials
**Activity:** Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems: The Three-Body Problem with Earth-Moon-Satellite Dynamics (90 min)

### Week 10: Quantum Heat Engines and Thermodynamic Limits
**Topics:** Quantum Carnot engines, quantum coherence effects
**Module:** Photoelectric Effect - emission of electrons from a material when light strikes its surface, demonstrating particle nature of light
**Module:** Work Function - minimum energy required to remove an electron from a material's surface, measured in electron volts (eV)

### Week 11: Oscillatory Thermal Systems and Resonance
**Topics:** Thermoacoustic engines, thermal oscillations
**Module:** Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) - periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium (F = -kx)
**Module:** Period (T) and Frequency (f) - time for one complete oscillation and number of oscillations per unit time, related by f = 1/T

### Week 12: Electromagnetic Interference in Thermal Management
**Topics:** EMI effects on electronic thermal management, shielding strategies
**Activity:** Analyzing Electromagnetic Interference in Multi-Frequency Circuit Systems (120 min)

### Week 13: Advanced System Design and Optimization
**Topics:** Multi-objective optimization, sustainability considerations
**Activity:** Analyzing Multi-Loop Circuit Breakdown: Kirchhoff's Laws Application (130 min)

### Week 14: Capstone Project Presentations
**Assessment:** Advanced Quantum Mechanics Phenomenon Analysis and Research Presentation (Presentation - 100 points)

### Week 15: Future Technologies and Course Integration
**Topics:** Emerging thermal technologies, course synthesis
**Assessment:** Quantum Mechanics Interpretation Debate: Copenhagen vs Many-Worlds vs Hidden Variables (Discussion - 100 points)

Students will explore the experimental evidence that established the Standard Model, from the discovery of quarks through deep inelastic scattering to the recent Higgs boson detection at the LHC. The course emphasizes hands-on analysis of real experimental data from major particle physics facilities including Fermilab, CERN, and KEK. Students will work with Monte Carlo simulations, learn to identify particle signatures in detector readouts, and understand the statistical methods used to claim discoveries. A major capstone project involves analyzing authentic data sets to either confirm known particle properties or search for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
• Analyze authentic particle physics data to identify experimental signatures of Standard Model particles including quarks, leptons, and bosons
• Design and execute a capstone research project using Monte Carlo simulations and statistical analysis techniques to investigate particle physics phenomena

• Synthesize theoretical predictions with experimental observations to evaluate the validity of particle physics models

course_info.title: Wireless Power and Communication Systems: Electromagnetic Field Engineering
course_info.description: This course explores the electromagnetic principles underlying modern wireless technologies, from smartphone charging pads to satellite communications. Students will design and analyze real-world electromagnetic systems including wireless power transfer coils, antenna arrays, and electromagnetic interference shielding. Through hands-on laboratory projects, students will build functional wireless charging systems, optimize antenna designs for specific frequency bands, and solve electromagnetic compatibility problems in electronic devices. The course emphasizes practical applications of Maxwell's equations, transmission line theory, and electromagnetic wave propagation in contemporary technology. Students will work with industry-standard simulation software and measurement equipment to characterize electromagnetic fields, design impedance matching networks, and evaluate SAR (Specific Absorption Rate) compliance for consumer electronics. Case studies include Tesla's wireless power experiments, RFID tag design, microwave oven safety systems, and 5G beamforming technologies. The curriculum integrates electromagnetic theory with materials science, examining how metamaterials and ferrites enhance device performance. Final projects involve proposing novel electromagnetic solutions to current engineering challenges, such as wireless EV charging infrastructure or IoT sensor networks with energy harvesting capabilities.

# Spacetime Navigation and GPS Technology: Relativistic Effects in Modern Positioning Systems

**Course Code:** PHYS 485  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** PHYS 301 (Modern Physics), PHYS 221 (Electricity & Magnetism), MATH 264 (Differential Equations)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM + Lab W 2:00-4:50 PM  
**Semester:** Spring 2024  

---

## Course Description

This applied physics course examines how Einstein's theories of special and general relativity are essential for the accurate functioning of Global Positioning Systems (GPS) and other satellite-based navigation technologies. Students explore how time dilation, gravitational redshift, and spacetime curvature create measurable errors in satellite timing that must be corrected for precise positioning. The course combines theoretical understanding of relativistic effects with hands-on analysis of real GPS data, satellite orbital mechanics, and error correction algorithms. Topics include the relativistic Doppler effect in moving satellites, gravitational time dilation at different altitudes, Sagnac effect corrections for Earth's rotation, and the integration of atomic clocks in space-based systems. Students work with actual GPS receiver data, analyze timing discrepancies, and develop correction protocols. Laboratory sessions involve programming relativistic corrections, comparing theoretical predictions with measured satellite data, and designing improved positioning algorithms. The course culminates in a project where students propose enhancements to current navigation systems or explore relativistic effects in emerging technologies like autonomous vehicles, precision agriculture, or interplanetary navigation systems.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Calculate relativistic time dilation and frequency shifts affecting GPS satellite signals and apply corrections to improve positioning accuracy  
• Analyze real GPS data to identify and quantify relativistic effects, developing practical skills in satellite navigation error analysis  
• Design and implement relativistic correction algorithms for positioning systems and evaluate their effectiveness in various technological applications  

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Course Introduction & GPS Fundamentals
**Topics:** Course overview, GPS system architecture, basic positioning principles, introduction to relativistic effects in navigation
**Reading:** Chapters 1-2 of course text

### Week 2: Special Relativity Review
**Module:** Simple Harmonic Motion: Springs, Pendulums, and Oscillations
- Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) - periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium (F = -kx)
- Period (T) and Frequency (f) - time for one complete oscillation and number of oscillations per unit time, related by f = 1/T

**Topics:** Time dilation, length contraction, Lorentz transformations, clock synchronization

### Week 3: General Relativity Foundations
**Topics:** Equivalence principle, gravitational time dilation, spacetime curvature, metric tensor basics
**Reading:** Chapter 3

### Week 4: Electromagnetic Foundations for GPS
**Module:** Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law
- Magnetic Flux (Φ): The measure of magnetic field lines passing through a surface, calculated as Φ = B⃗ · A⃗ = BA cos θ
- Faraday's Law: The induced EMF equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt

### Week 5: Wave Propagation and Signal Analysis
**Module:** Wave Interference and Superposition Phenomena
- Principle of Superposition - waves combine algebraically when overlapping, with the resultant displacement being the sum of individual wave displacements
- Constructive Interference - waves combine to produce maximum amplitude when their phase difference is zero or multiples of 2π

### Week 6: Satellite Orbital Mechanics
**Topics:** Kepler's laws, orbital periods, gravitational potential at satellite altitudes, velocity calculations
**Assessment:Quiz - Advanced Quantum Mechanics and Electromagnetic Theory Comprehensive Quiz** (100 points)

### Week 7: Time Dilation in GPS Satellites
**Topics:** Special relativistic effects from satellite motion (~7 μs/day advance), velocity-dependent time dilation calculations
**Reading:** Chapter 5

### Week 8: Gravitational Time Dilation Effects  
**Topics:** General relativistic effects from gravitational potential difference (~45 μs/day delay), altitude-dependent corrections

### Week 9: Mid-Semester Break & Exam Preparation
**Assessment:Exam - Advanced Quantum Mechanics and Electromagnetic Theory Comprehensive Exam** (100 points)

### Week 10: Doppler Shifts and Frequency Analysis
**Topics:** Relativistic Doppler effect, frequency shifts in satellite signals, carrier phase measurements

### Week 11: Sagnac Effect and Earth's Rotation
**Topics:** Frame dragging, rotating reference frames, Sagnac correction for Earth's rotation
**Reading:** Chapter 7

### Week 12: Atomic Clocks and Precision Timekeeping
**Module:** Wave-Particle Duality and the Photoelectric Effect  
- Photoelectric Effect - emission of electrons from a material when light strikes its surface, demonstrating particle nature of light
- Work Function - minimum energy required to remove an electron from a material's surface, measured in electron volts (eV)

### Week 13: Error Analysis and Correction Algorithms
**Topics:** GPS error sources, multipath effects, atmospheric delays, relativistic correction implementation
**Assessment:Discussion - Quantum Mechanics Interpretations: Copenhagen vs Many-Worlds Analysis** (100 points)

### Week 14: Advanced Applications and Future Technologies
**Topics:** Precision agriculture, autonomous vehicles, interplanetary navigation, next-generation positioning systems

### Week 15: Student Presentations
**Assessment:Presentation - Advanced Quantum Mechanics Research Presentation: Theoretical Analysis and Experimental Applications** (100 points)
**Topics:** Student project presentations on GPS enhancements or emerging navigation technologies

### Week 16: Course Wrap-up and Portfolio Submission
**Assessment:Portfolio - Advanced Physics Research Portfolio: Investigating Complex Physical Phenomena** (100 points)
**Topics:** Course review, career applications, research opportunities

course_info.description: This advanced undergraduate course explores the fundamental relationship between symmetries and conservation laws in particle physics, building from Noether's theorem to modern gauge theories. Students investigate how spatial, temporal, and internal symmetries govern particle interactions through the Standard Model framework. The course emphasizes hands-on analysis of experimental data from particle accelerators, examining how symmetry breaking mechanisms give rise to particle masses and mixing phenomena. Key topics include discrete symmetries (C, P, T), continuous symmetries (rotational, translational, gauge), spontaneous symmetry breaking via the Higgs mechanism, and CP violation in weak interactions. Laboratory components involve analyzing real collision data from CERN and Fermilab to identify particle signatures and measure fundamental parameters. Students develop computational skills using ROOT software for data analysis and Monte Carlo simulations. The course culminates in independent research projects investigating current puzzles in particle physics, such as the matter-antimatter asymmetry problem or dark matter candidates. This specialized approach bridges theoretical foundations with experimental techniques, preparing students for graduate research in high-energy physics or careers in accelerator-based research facilities.

# PHYS 4850: Symmetries and Conservation Laws in High-Energy Particle Interactions

---

## INSTRUCTOR INFORMATION

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This advanced undergraduate course explores the fundamental relationship between symmetries and conservation laws in particle physics, building from Noether's theorem to modern gauge theories. Students investigate how spatial, temporal, and internal symmetries govern particle interactions through the Standard Model framework. The course emphasizes hands-on analysis of experimental data from particle accelerators, examining how symmetry breaking mechanisms give rise to particle masses and mixing phenomena. Key topics include discrete symmetries (C, P, T), continuous symmetries (rotational, translational, gauge), spontaneous symmetry breaking via the Higgs mechanism, and CP violation in weak interactions. Laboratory components involve analyzing real collision data from CERN and Fermilab to identify particle signatures and measure fundamental parameters. Students develop computational skills using ROOT software for data analysis and Monte Carlo simulations. The course culminates in independent research projects investigating current puzzles in particle physics, such as the matter-antimatter asymmetry problem or dark matter candidates.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master the mathematical framework** connecting symmetry principles to conservation laws in particle interactions and apply group theory concepts to analyze particle multiplets and decay processes

2. **Apply specialized computational techniques** including ROOT data analysis software and Monte Carlo methods to interpret real experimental particle physics data from major accelerator facilities

3. **Develop practical expertise** in identifying particle signatures, calculating cross-sections, and designing experiments to test symmetry violations in high-energy collision processes

# **PHYS 2450: The Quantum Zoo: Exploring Nature's Fundamental Building BlocksCourse Information**

- **Prerequisites:** PHYS 2020 (General Physics II) or equivalent

- **Semester:** Spring 2024

---

## **Course Description**

Journey into the subatomic world to discover the elementary particles that comprise all matter and energy in the universe. This course provides an accessible introduction to particle physics, exploring quarks, leptons, bosons, and their interactions through the four fundamental forces. Students will learn about particle classification systems, conservation laws, and detection methods used in modern experiments. The course emphasizes conceptual understanding over advanced mathematics, using analogies, visual models, and interactive simulations to make abstract concepts tangible. Topics include the Standard Model of particle physics, antimatter, particle accelerators, cosmic rays, and recent discoveries like the Higgs boson. Students will analyze real experimental data from facilities like CERN and explore how particle physics connects to cosmology, energy production, and medical applications. Laboratory sessions feature cloud chamber construction, radiation detection, and computer simulations of particle collisions. By course completion, students will understand how physicists probe nature's smallest scales and appreciate the elegant mathematical framework underlying physical reality.

## **Learning Objectives**

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
1. Classify fundamental particles using quantum numbers and identify their roles in the Standard Model framework
2. Apply conservation laws to analyze particle interactions and decay processes in collision experiments
3. Interpret detector data and explain how modern particle physics experiments reveal properties of subatomic particles

---

## **Weekly Schedule**

### **Week 1: Course Introduction & FoundationsTopics:** Course overview, historical development of atomic theory, scale of the subatomic world
**Module:** Newton's Laws of Motion: Forces and Dynamics
- Inertia and its role in particle motion
- Net force concepts in particle interactions

### **Week 2: Energy and MatterTopics:** Mass-energy equivalence, relativistic effects in particle physics
**Module:** Conservation of Energy and Work-Energy Theorem
- Kinetic energy in high-speed particle collisions
- Gravitational potential energy in cosmic ray interactions

### **Week 3: The Quantum Nature of Light and MatterTopics:** Photons, wave-particle duality, quantum mechanics basics
**Module:** Wave-Particle Duality and the Photoelectric Effect
- Photon energy quantization in particle detection
- Work function applications in particle detectors

### **Week 4: Wave Properties in Quantum SystemsTopics:** Matter waves, uncertainty principle, probability waves
**Module:** Wave Interference and Superposition
- Superposition principle in quantum mechanics
- Constructive interference in wave functions

### **Week 5: Quantum Tunneling and BarriersTopics:** Barrier penetration, alpha decay, nuclear physics applications
**Module:** Wave Interference and Standing Wave Patterns
- Wave behavior in confined systems
- Standing wave patterns in atomic orbitals

### **Week 6: Detection Methods I - Electromagnetic PrinciplesTopics:** Particle detectors, ionization chambers, scintillators
**Module:** Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law (Version 1)
- Magnetic flux in detector design
- Faraday's law in electromagnetic calorimeters

### **Week 7: Detection Methods II - Advanced DetectorsTopics:** Wire chambers, silicon detectors, calorimeters
**Module:** Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law (Version 2)
- Magnetic flux applications in tracking detectors
- Induced EMF in detector readout systems

### **Week 8: The Standard Model FrameworkTopics:** Particle classification, quarks, leptons, fundamental interactions
**Module:** Wave Interference and Superposition (Review)
- Quantum state superposition in particle physics
- Interference effects in particle interactions

### **Week 9: Quarks and the Strong ForceTopics:** Quark flavors, color charge, gluons, confinement
**Module:** Wave Interference and Standing Waves
- Quantum chromodynamics wave functions
- Resonance patterns in quark-gluon interactions

### **Week 10: Leptons and the Weak ForceTopics:** Electron, muon, tau families, neutrinos, weak interactions
**Module:** Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law (Version 3)
- Electromagnetic signatures of weak decays
- Flux calculations in neutrino detection

### **Week 11: Bosons and Force CarriersTopics:** Photons, W and Z bosons, gluons, the Higgs mechanism

### **Week 12: Symmetries and Conservation LawsTopics:** Conservation of energy, momentum, charge, and quantum numbers in particle interactions

### **Week 13: Particle Accelerators and CollidersTopics:** Linear accelerators, synchrotrons, colliding beam experiments, CERN and other facilities

### **Week 14: Antimatter and CP ViolationTopics:** Antiparticles, matter-antimatter asymmetry, CP violation, cosmological implications

### **Week 15: Frontiers and ApplicationsTopics:** Beyond the Standard Model, dark matter, medical applications, future experiments

### **Week 16: Final Projects and ReviewTopics:** Student presentations, course synthesis, current research frontiers

# ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVE ENGINEERING AND ANTENNA DESIGN
**Course Code:** PHYS 485 | **Credits:** 4 | **Semester:** Fall 2024  
**Prerequisites:** PHYS 380 (Electromagnetic Theory), MATH 340 (Differential Equations)

## INSTRUCTOR INFORMATION

**Teaching Assistant:** [TA Name]  
**TA Email:** [TA Email]  
**Lab Sections:** [Times and Locations]

## COURSE DESCRIPTION
This hands-on course explores the practical applications of electromagnetic theory in modern communication and sensing systems. Students will bridge theoretical Maxwell's equations with real-world engineering challenges, focusing on electromagnetic wave propagation, transmission line theory, and antenna design principles. The course emphasizes laboratory work where students design, build, and test various antenna configurations including dipoles, Yagi-Uda arrays, and microstrip antennas. Projects involve using vector network analyzers, spectrum analyzers, and electromagnetic simulation software to characterize antenna performance parameters such as radiation patterns, gain, and impedance matching. Students will explore applications in wireless communications, radar systems, satellite technology, and emerging 5G/6G networks. By semester's end, students complete a capstone project designing an antenna system for a specific application, considering factors like frequency response, bandwidth, polarization, and environmental durability.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master electromagnetic wave propagation principles** and apply Maxwell's equations to solve practical antenna design problems
2. **Apply transmission line theory and Smith chart analysis** to design impedance matching networks and optimize antenna performance  
3. **Develop practical expertise** in electromagnetic simulation tools and laboratory measurement techniques for characterizing antenna systems

## REQUIRED MATERIALS
- **Textbook:** "Antenna Theory: Analysis and Design" by Constantine A. Balanis (4th Edition)
- **Supplemental Text:** "Fields and Waves in Communication Electronics" by Ramo, Whinnery, and Van Duzer
- **Software:** HFSS, CST Studio Suite, or equivalent EM simulation software (provided in lab)
- **Laboratory:** Safety glasses, laboratory notebook, USB drive for data storage

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Foundations of Electromagnetic Induction
**Module:** Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law  
**Key Concepts:**
- Magnetic Flux (Φ): The measure of magnetic field lines passing through a surface, calculated as Φ = B⃗ · A⃗ = BA cos θ
- Faraday's Law: The induced EMF equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt

**Activities:**
- Electromagnetic Induction Analysis: Deconstructing Faraday's Law in Complex Multi-Coil Systems (160 min)

### Week 2: Wave Fundamentals and Superposition
**Module:** Wave Interference and Superposition: Understanding Constructive and Destructive Wave Interactions  
**Key Concepts:**
- Principle of Superposition: Mathematical rule for wave overlap where resultant displacement equals algebraic sum of individual wave displacements
- Phase Difference: The difference in phase between two waves, determining constructive or destructive interference

**Activities:**
- Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Slit Diffraction Systems (120 min)

### Week 3-4: Maxwell's Equations and EM Wave Propagation
**Lectures:** 
- Maxwell's equations in differential and integral form
- Wave equation derivation from Maxwell's equations
- Plane wave solutions and boundary conditions
- Poynting vector and energy flow

### Week 5-6: Transmission Lines and Impedance Matching
**Lectures:**
- Transmission line theory and telegrapher's equations
- Standing wave patterns and VSWR
- Smith chart analysis and applications
- Quarter-wave transformers and stub matching

### Week 7-8: Fundamental Antenna Principles
**Lectures:**
- Radiation mechanism and near/far field regions
- Antenna parameters: gain, directivity, efficiency, bandwidth
- Reciprocity theorem and antenna measurements
- Linear and circular polarization

**Assessment:** Advanced Electromagnetic Induction Lab Report (Due Week 8)

### Week 9-10: Wire Antennas and Arrays
**Lectures:**
- Hertzian dipole and finite-length dipoles
- Monopole antennas and ground plane effects
- Yagi-Uda arrays and beam steering
- Phased array fundamentals

### Week 11-12: Aperture and Microstrip Antennas
**Lectures:**
- Horn antennas and aperture efficiency
- Parabolic reflectors and feed systems
- Microstrip patch antennas
- Antenna miniaturization techniques

### Week 13-14: Advanced Topics and Applications
**Lectures:**
- MIMO antenna systems
- 5G/6G antenna technologies
- Metamaterial antennas
- Regulatory compliance and SAR considerations

**Activities:**
- Multi-Variable Circuit Analysis: Complex Network Decomposition (120 min)
- Electromagnetic Spectrum Analysis Project (100 min)

### Week 15: Final Projects and Presentations
**Capstone Project PresentationsFinal Exam Review**

## ASSESSMENT PLAN

# Data-Driven Application Architecture: Building Scalable Software Systems

**Course Code:** CS 485  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** CS 245 (Database Systems), CS 335 (Software Engineering)  
**Meeting Time:** Tuesdays & Thursdays, 3:30-5:00 PM  
**Semester:** Spring 2024  

---

## Course Description

This intensive, project-based course focuses on designing and implementing software applications with robust database foundations. Students will learn to architect scalable systems by mastering database design patterns, query optimization, and data persistence strategies across multiple database paradigms. The course emphasizes real-world application development through hands-on projects that integrate relational databases, NoSQL solutions, and modern data storage technologies. 

Students will work with industry-standard tools including PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, and cloud database services while building full-stack applications. Key topics include database normalization, indexing strategies, transaction management, data modeling for different use cases, API design for data access, caching mechanisms, and performance tuning. 

The curriculum is structured around three major projects: an e-commerce platform with complex product catalogs, a social media analytics dashboard, and a real-time chat application with message persistence. Students will also explore emerging trends like graph databases, time-series data management, and microservices data architecture. By course completion, students will have developed a portfolio of database-driven applications and gained practical experience in making architectural decisions that balance performance, scalability, and maintainability in modern software systems.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Database Design & Optimization:** Design and implement normalized relational database schemas and optimize query performance for complex business requirements
2. **Multi-Paradigm Persistence:** Architect data persistence layers using multiple database technologies (SQL, NoSQL, in-memory) based on specific application needs
3. **Full-Stack Integration:** Develop full-stack applications that demonstrate advanced database integration patterns including connection pooling, transaction management, and caching strategies
4. **Scalability Solutions:** Evaluate and implement database scaling solutions including replication, sharding, and cloud-based database services for production environments
5. **API Development:** Create comprehensive data access APIs that follow RESTful principles while ensuring data security and integrity

### **Week 5-6: Advanced API ImplementationModule:** API Design and Implementation with RESTful Services

### **Week 11-12: Project 2 - Social Media Analytics DashboardFocus:** NoSQL and Real-time Data Processing

- Time-series data handling
- Real-time data visualization techniques

**Activities:**

- **Assessment:** My First Web Application: Design and Development Presentation (Week 12)

### **Week 13-14: Project 3 - Real-time Chat ApplicationFocus:** Advanced Architecture Patterns

**Prerequisites:** CS 2020 (Object-Oriented Programming), CS 2030 (Data Structures)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM

## Instructor Information

## Course Description
This foundational course explores the complete lifecycle of mobile application development across iOS and Android platforms, emphasizing architectural patterns, user experience design, and deployment strategies. Students will learn core concepts of mobile app development including native vs. hybrid approaches, responsive UI/UX design principles, data persistence, API integration, and mobile-specific security considerations. The course combines theoretical foundations with hands-on projects using modern cross-platform frameworks like React Native and Flutter. Students will develop multiple mobile applications from conception to deployment, learning version control, testing methodologies, app store optimization, and performance monitoring. Key topics include mobile hardware constraints, battery optimization, offline functionality, push notifications, and monetization strategies. The curriculum emphasizes industry best practices for code organization, component reusability, and scalable architecture design. Students will also explore emerging trends in mobile development including progressive web apps, augmented reality integration, and IoT connectivity. By course completion, students will have built a portfolio of functional mobile applications and gained comprehensive understanding of the mobile development ecosystem, preparing them for advanced coursework or entry-level positions in mobile application development.

# Cross-Platform Framework Architecture: Building Scalable Applications with React Native, Flutter, and Xamarin

**Course Code:** CS 485  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 320 (Mobile Application Development), CS 315 (Software Engineering)  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

---

## Course Description

This specialized course examines the architectural patterns and implementation strategies of three major cross-platform mobile development frameworks. Students will dive deep into React Native's bridge architecture, Flutter's widget-based rendering engine, and Xamarin's native API bindings. The course emphasizes comparative analysis of framework performance, memory management, and platform-specific optimizations. Through hands-on projects, students will build identical applications across all three frameworks, analyzing trade-offs in development speed, code reusability, and native performance. Advanced topics include custom native module development, framework interoperability, CI/CD pipeline integration, and enterprise deployment strategies. Students will also explore emerging trends like React Native's new architecture (Fabric and TurboModules), Flutter's desktop expansion, and Microsoft's .NET MAUI evolution. The course culminates in a capstone project where teams architect a complex cross-platform solution, making framework selection decisions based on specific business requirements, team expertise, and technical constraints.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master architectural patterns and core concepts** of React Native, Flutter, and Xamarin frameworks  
• **Apply comparative analysis methodologies** to evaluate framework performance, scalability, and development efficiency  
• **Develop expertise in cross-platform deployment strategies**, native module integration, and framework-specific optimization techniques  

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Course Introduction and Cross-Platform Landscape
**Topics:**
- Course overview and expectations
- Evolution of mobile development
- Cross-platform vs. native development paradigms
- Framework ecosystem comparison

**Readings:** Course syllabus, Framework comparison whitepaper

### Week 2: React Native Architecture Fundamentals

- Bridge architecture and JavaScript thread
- Component lifecycle and state management
- Metro bundler and development workflow
- Platform-specific implementations

**Readings:** React Native Documentation (Architecture Overview)

### Week 3: React Native Development Deep Dive
**Module:** Test-Driven Development (TDD) with JavaScript  
**Key Concepts:**
- Red-Green-Refactor Cycle - The three-phase TDD process of writing failing tests, making them pass, then improving code quality
- Unit Testing - Testing individual functions or components in isolation to verify they behave correctly for given inputs

**Activity:** Code Review Battle: Evaluating Bug-Prone JavaScript Functions (60 minutes)

### Week 4: Flutter Architecture and Widget System
**Topics:**
- Dart VM and Flutter engine
- Widget tree and rendering pipeline
- State management patterns (setState, Provider, BLoC)
- Hot reload and development experience

**Readings:** Flutter Documentation (Architecture Overview)

### Week 5: Flutter Advanced Concepts and Performance
**Topics:**
- Custom widgets and painting
- Platform channels and method channels
- Memory management and performance optimization
- Flutter Inspector tools

### Week 6: Xamarin and .NET MAUI Architecture
**Topics:**
- Xamarin.Forms vs. Xamarin.Native
- .NET runtime and platform abstractions
- XAML and data binding patterns
- Migration to .NET MAUI

**Readings:** Microsoft Documentation (.NET MAUI Architecture)

### Week 7: Framework Comparison Project - Phase 1
**Module:** Test-Driven Development (TDD) Implementation and Best Practices  
**Key Concepts:**
- Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The three-phase TDD process of writing failing tests, making them pass, and improving code structure
- Unit Testing Frameworks: Tools like Jest (JavaScript) and JUnit (Java) that provide structure and utilities for writing and running tests

**Activity:** Code Review and Quality Assessment: Evaluating Simple Calculator Functions (50 minutes)

**Assessment:** Personal Task Manager Web Application (Project) - 100 points

### Week 8: Native Module Development and Platform Integration
**Topics:**
- Creating custom React Native modules
- Writing Flutter plugins
- Xamarin platform-specific implementations
- Platform channel communication patterns

### Week 9: Performance Analysis and Optimization
**Module:** API Design and RESTful Web Services  
**Key Concepts:**
- REST (Representational State Transfer) - Architectural style for distributed systems emphasizing stateless communication and resource-based URLs
- HTTP Methods - GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH operations that define actions performed on API resources

**Topics:**
- Memory profiling and leak detection
- Rendering performance optimization
- Bundle size analysis and optimization
- Battery usage and power efficiency

### Week 10: Testing Strategies and Quality Assurance
**Module:** Test-Driven Development (TDD) with Unit Testing Frameworks  
**Key Concepts:**
- Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD workflow of writing a failing test (Red), implementing minimal code to pass (Green), and improving code quality (Refactor)
- Test Doubles: Mock objects, stubs, and fakes used to isolate the unit under test from external dependencies and control test environments

**Activity:** Code Quality Detective: Evaluating Beginner Python Functions (85 minutes)

**Assessment:** Software Development Fundamentals Quiz - 100 points

### Week 11: CI/CD Pipeline Integration and DevOps
**Topics:**
- Automated testing across frameworks
- Build pipeline configuration
- Code signing and deployment strategies
- App store submission processes

### Week 12: Enterprise Deployment and Security
**Topics:**
- Enterprise app distribution
- Security considerations and best practices
- Code obfuscation and protection
- Analytics and crash reporting integration

**Assessment:** Personal Website Portfolio - HTML, CSS, and JavaScript Fundamentals (Portfolio) - 100 points

### Week 13: Emerging Technologies and Future Trends
**Topics:**
- React Native's Fabric and TurboModules
- Flutter for web and desktop
- WebAssembly and cross-platform compilation
- Comparative market analysis

**Activity:** Bug Fix Solution Evaluation: Comparing and Critiquing Different Approaches (55 minutes)

course_info.description: This survey course explores the modern software delivery landscape, examining how applications journey from developer workstations to production environments. Students investigate diverse deployment pipelines, infrastructure paradigms, and operational practices across different technology stacks and organizational contexts. **Prerequisites:** Data Structures and Algorithms, Database Systems  
**Meeting Time:** TTh 2:00-3:15 PM

---

## Course Description

This survey course explores the modern software delivery landscape, examining how applications journey from developer workstations to production environments. Students investigate diverse deployment pipelines, infrastructure paradigms, and operational practices across different technology stacks and organizational contexts. The course provides broad exposure to containerization technologies, cloud platforms, monitoring systems, and automation frameworks without deep specialization in any single tool. Through hands-on labs and case studies, students compare GitLab CI/CD versus GitHub Actions, explore Kubernetes alongside traditional server deployments, and analyze real-world incident response scenarios. Topics include infrastructure as code, observability patterns, security integration, and deployment strategies ranging from blue-green to canary releases. Students examine how DevOps practices vary across startups, enterprises, and open-source projects, developing critical thinking about tool selection and process design. The survey approach emphasizes understanding the 'why' behind different approaches rather than becoming expert practitioners, preparing students to adapt to rapidly evolving deployment technologies and make informed architectural decisions in their future careers.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Evaluate and compare** major DevOps tools, platforms, and methodologies used across different organizational contexts

# Quality Assurance Engineering: Building Bulletproof Software Systems

**Course Code:** CS 4XX  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** CS 3XX (Software Engineering), CS 2XX (Data Structures and Algorithms)  
**Semester:** Spring 2024  
**Meeting Time:** Tuesday/Thursday 2:00-3:50 PM  

## Course Description

This capstone course transforms students into quality assurance engineers who design, implement, and maintain comprehensive testing ecosystems for real-world software projects. Students work with industry partners to diagnose, repair, and fortify existing software systems while building automated testing pipelines from scratch. The course emphasizes test-driven development, continuous integration, performance testing, and security vulnerability assessment. Teams manage complete QA lifecycles including requirements analysis, test planning, defect tracking, and quality metrics reporting. Students develop expertise in modern testing frameworks, create custom testing tools, and implement monitoring solutions for production environments. The capstone project involves partnering with a local business or open-source project to conduct a full quality audit, implement comprehensive testing strategies, and deliver a production-ready quality assurance framework. By semester's end, students present their QA solutions to industry professionals and demonstrate measurable improvements in software reliability, performance, and security. This hands-on experience bridges academic learning with professional QA engineering practices, preparing graduates for immediate impact in software quality roles.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Architect and implement end-to-end automated testing pipelines using industry-standard frameworks and continuous integration tools  
• Conduct comprehensive quality audits of real-world software systems and develop actionable improvement strategies for industry partners  
• Master advanced testing methodologies including performance benchmarking, security penetration testing, and user acceptance validation  
• Design and deploy production-grade monitoring and alerting systems to ensure ongoing software quality and reliability  
• Demonstrate professional QA communication skills through detailed defect reporting, stakeholder presentations, and quality metrics documentation

## Required Materials

- **Textbook:** "The Art of Software Testing" by Glenford Myers (3rd Edition)
- **Software:** Access to GitHub, Jenkins, Docker, and various testing frameworks
- **Hardware:** Laptop capable of running development environments
- **Industry Partnership:** Students will be matched with local businesses or open-source projects

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1-2: Foundations of Quality Assurance
**Module:** Test-Driven Development (TDD) Fundamentals
- Red-Green-Refactor Cycle - The three-phase TDD process of writing failing tests, implementing minimal code, and improving design
- Unit Testing Frameworks - Tools like JUnit, pytest, or Mocha that provide structure and assertions for automated testing

**Activities:**
- Code Quality Detective: Evaluating Beginner Python Functions (60 minutes)
- Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes and Code Improvements (45 minutes)

### Week 3-4: Advanced TDD Implementation
**Module:** Test-Driven Development (TDD) Implementation and Best Practices
- Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD workflow of writing failing tests, implementing minimal code to pass, then improving design through refactoring
- Test Coverage: Measurement of how much source code is executed during testing, including statement, branch, and path coverage metrics

**Activities:**
- Evaluating Code Quality: Simple Calculator Function Assessment (45 minutes)
- Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program (50 minutes)

### Week 5-6: JavaScript Testing Ecosystem
**Module:** Test-Driven Development (TDD) with JavaScript and Jest
- Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The three-phase TDD process of writing failing tests (Red), making tests pass (Green), and improving code structure (Refactor)
- Test Coverage: Measurement of how much source code is executed during testing, including line, branch, and function coverage metrics

**Activities:**
- Code Review Battle: Evaluating Bug-Prone JavaScript Functions (60 minutes)
- Code Review and Quality Assessment: Evaluating Simple Calculator Functions (50 minutes)

### Week 7-8: Test Doubles and Mocking

- Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD workflow of writing a failing test (Red), implementing minimal code to pass (Green), and improving code quality (Refactor)
- Test Doubles: Mock objects, stubs, and fakes used to isolate the unit under test from external dependencies and control test environments

**Activities:**
- Evaluating Password Validation Functions: Security vs. Usability Trade-offs (90 minutes)
- Code Review Evaluation: Comparing Two Password Validation Solutions (85 minutes)

**Assessment:** Software Development Fundamentals Quiz (Due Week 8)

### Week 9-10: API Testing and Integration

- REST (Representational State Transfer) - Architectural style for distributed systems emphasizing stateless communication and resource-based URLs
- HTTP Methods - GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH operations that define actions performed on API resources

**Activities:**
- Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program (60 minutes)

**Assessment:** Basic Web Application Development Exam (Week 10)

**Focus:** Building automated testing pipelines, CI/CD integration, and deployment testing strategies

### Week 13-14: Performance and Security Testing
**Focus:** Load testing, security vulnerability assessment, penetration testing methodologies

**Assessment:** Personal Portfolio Website Development Project (Due Week 14)

# Cross-Platform Mobile Development: From Concept to App Store

**Course Code:** CS 385  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Programming Fundamentals (CS 201), Object-Oriented Programming (CS 202)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM + Lab: W 2:00-3:50 PM

## Course Description

This foundational course guides students through the complete lifecycle of mobile application development using cross-platform frameworks. Students begin by exploring mobile app ecosystems, user experience principles specific to mobile interfaces, and market analysis techniques. The course emphasizes hands-on development using React Native and Flutter, enabling students to create applications that run seamlessly on both iOS and Android platforms. Core topics include mobile UI/UX design patterns, responsive layouts, device-specific features (camera, GPS, sensors), data persistence, API integration, and performance optimization. Students learn industry-standard development practices including version control with Git, automated testing, debugging techniques, and deployment strategies. The curriculum balances theoretical foundations with practical project work, culminating in students developing, testing, and preparing their own mobile applications for app store submission.

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master cross-platform mobile development frameworks** to create native-quality applications for iOS and Android platforms  
• **Apply mobile-first design principles** and user experience methodologies to develop intuitive, accessible mobile interfaces  
• **Develop practical expertise** in mobile app deployment, testing, and app store optimization strategies

**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 250 (Software Engineering) or equivalent  
**Semester:** Spring 2024  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  

---

## Course Description

This comprehensive survey course examines the complete software delivery lifecycle through the lens of modern DevOps practices and toolchains. Students explore how software moves from developer workstations to production environments, investigating the intersection of development, operations, security, and quality assurance. The course provides broad exposure to containerization technologies, continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, infrastructure as code, monitoring and observability, and cloud deployment strategies. Through hands-on labs and case studies from industry leaders like Netflix, Google, and Amazon, students gain practical experience with tools such as Docker, Kubernetes, Jenkins, Git workflows, and cloud platforms. The survey approach ensures students understand not just individual tools, but how they integrate into cohesive delivery ecosystems. Topics include automated testing strategies, release management, incident response, performance optimization, and security integration throughout the development process. Students will analyze real-world deployment architectures, compare different organizational approaches to DevOps adoption, and evaluate trade-offs between various tools and methodologies. By course completion, students will possess a comprehensive understanding of modern software delivery practices and the ability to design efficient, reliable deployment pipelines.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Analyze and compare** various CI/CD pipeline architectures and their implementation across different organizational contexts

## Course Description

Through collaborative projects, students will build distributed applications that demonstrate modern software integration patterns, working with containerized services, event-driven architectures, and third-party API integrations. Students will gain expertise in API documentation, testing strategies, monitoring, and performance optimization. The curriculum covers emerging trends including serverless APIs, webhook systems, and API monetization models. By course completion, students will have developed a portfolio showcasing their ability to create scalable, maintainable software systems that leverage APIs as fundamental building blocks for modern application development.

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Design and implement comprehensive API architectures** using REST, GraphQL, and event-driven patterns for scalable software systems
2. **Apply industry-standard practices** for API lifecycle management including versioning, documentation, testing, and monitoring in production environments
3. **Develop expertise in building distributed applications** through microservices communication, API gateways, and third-party service integrations

# Building Scalable Web Applications with Modern JavaScript Ecosystems
**Course Code:** CS 4XX | **Credits:** 3 | **Semester:** Spring 2024

## Course Description

This intensive, project-driven course immerses students in the complete lifecycle of developing production-ready web applications using contemporary JavaScript frameworks and tools. Students will architect, build, and deploy full-stack applications while mastering React, Node.js, and cloud deployment strategies. The curriculum emphasizes real-world software engineering practices including automated testing, continuous integration, database design, API development, and performance optimization. 

Through collaborative team projects simulating industry environments, students will experience agile development methodologies, code reviews, and version control workflows. The course culminates in students launching live web applications that demonstrate proficiency in modern development practices, from initial wireframing through production deployment. 

Key technologies include React/Redux for frontend development, Express.js for backend APIs, MongoDB for data persistence, Docker for containerization, and AWS for cloud hosting. Students will also gain hands-on experience with development tools such as Jest for testing, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, and monitoring solutions for application health tracking.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement full-stack web applications using React, Node.js, and cloud-based deployment pipelines

# Building Interactive Web Applications: From Concept to Deployment
**CS 2350 | Fall 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## Course Description

This foundational course guides students through the complete lifecycle of creating modern web applications, emphasizing hands-on development and real-world problem-solving. Students will learn to build responsive, interactive web applications using contemporary technologies including HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and popular frameworks. The course covers essential concepts such as client-server architecture, RESTful APIs, database integration, and user experience design principles. Through project-based learning, students will develop a portfolio of web applications while mastering version control, testing methodologies, and deployment strategies. Special attention is given to accessibility standards, security best practices, and performance optimization. Students will work both individually and in teams to simulate industry development environments, learning collaborative coding practices and agile development methodologies. By the end of the semester, students will have created multiple fully-functional web applications and gained practical experience with cloud deployment platforms. The course balances theoretical understanding with practical application, ensuring students develop both the technical skills and professional practices necessary for modern web development careers.

---

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design and implement responsive web applications** using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and modern frameworks

• **Apply industry-standard development practices** including version control, testing, and deployment workflows
